summary: Target-level roadmap for completed group rings, canonical localization, characteristic classes, equivariant zeta objects and leading terms. Revision 2 reconstructs the corrected multiplicative-logarithm kernel/cokernel proof, replaces a false cyclic-overgroup congruence by full Möbius congruences and canonical descent of a completed zeta element, and types global leading terms on shifted complexes with corrected orders and cyclotomic normalization. All stages remain planned, not formally proved or source-leaf closed. Existing independent-review verdicts are unchanged historical records; this revision awaits independent review.

nodes.title: Uniform pro-p groups
nodes.statement: For prime p and a pro-p group U, write U^n for the closed subgroup generated by n-th powers. U is powerful when [U,U]⊆U^p for odd p, and [U,U]⊆U⁴ for p=2. A uniform group is a finitely generated powerful torsion-free pro-p group; equivalently its lower-p-series successive indices are constant. Its dimension d is the minimal number of topological generators, so |U:U^p|=p^d. The equivalence with the constant-index definition is part of this target.
hypotheses: p is prime; U is a Hausdorff compact pro-p group.
proofSteps: Import the closed lower p-series and p-adic powers from ProfiniteArithmetic, with P_i=λ_(i−1).
Use the uniform-group criterion cited in Ardakov–Brown §2.3 to compare torsion-freeness and constant indices; the nontrivial equivalence is a source gap until its primary proof is checked.
acceptance: ℤ_p^d is uniform of dimension d; the first congruence subgroup Γ₁(GL_d(ℤ_p)) (p odd) is uniform.
ℤ/p is powerful but not uniform (indices p, 1).

sources.match: Powerful, then uniform = powerful, finitely generated and |G : P₂| = |P_i : P_{i+1}|.

nodes.title: Compact p-adic analytic groups
nodes.statement: The group-side model of a compact p-adic analytic group is a profinite G containing an open normal uniform pro-p subgroup U. Its dimension is dim U, independent of U. The equivalence of this model with a compatible p-adic Lie-group structure is imported from the analytic-distributions owner (Schneider Theorems 27.1 and 29.8), rather than rebuilding an analytic atlas here.
hypotheses: The group-theoretic characterisation is taken as the definition. Its equivalence with a compatible analytic manifold group is supplied by NoncommutativeAnalyticDistributions; registering the exact supplier stage and checking the primary uniform-basis criterion remain explicit gaps.
proofSteps: Package: profinite (compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected) topological group with ∃ U open normal, pro-p and uniform.

Closure properties used later: open subgroups, closed normal subgroups and quotients by closed normal subgroups of compact p-adic analytic groups are compact p-adic analytic (Ardakov–Brown §2.1, citing Dixon–du Sautoy–Mann–Segal).
acceptance: Finite groups, ℤ_p^d × (finite), GL_d(ℤ_p), SL_d(ℤ_p) and their congruence subgroups are examples.
Separate: 'no element of order p', 'torsion-free' and 'pro-p' are different hypotheses (ℤ_p × ℤ/ℓ for ℓ ≠ p has no element of order p but is not pro-p; ℤ_p ⋊ ℤ/p may have p-torsion).

nodes.title: Completed group algebras are free over open subgroups
nodes.statement: Let G be profinite and H′ ≤ H closed subgroups with H′ open in H. Then Λ(H) is a free left (and right) Λ(H′)-module of rank [H : H′], with basis any set of right (resp. left) coset representatives; likewise Ω(H) over Ω(H′). If H′ is open normal in H, Λ(H) ≅ Λ(H′) ∗ (H/H′) is a crossed product. Consequently a Λ(H)-module is finitely generated over Λ(H) iff it is finitely generated over Λ(H′).
hypotheses: Λ(−) = ℤ_p⟦−⟧, Ω(−) = F_p⟦−⟧, the completed group algebras of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras L1.
proofSteps: Compute Λ(H) as lim ℤ_p[H/V] over open normal V ≤ H′ of H; at each level ℤ_p[H/V] is free over ℤ_p[H′/V] on coset representatives; the bases are compatible, so the limit is free on the same set.
Finite generation transfers because Λ(H) is finite free over Λ(H′).
acceptance: The basis is a set of coset representatives, independent of the level V.

For p=5, G=S₃×Z₅ and U=Z₅, Λ(G) is free of rank 6 over Λ(U). Its Γ-augmentation quotient is Z₅[S₃], where the basis products (12)(123) and (123)(12) differ. Commutative power series cannot replace this group ring.

nodes.statement: For a pro-p group G, Λ(G) is a compact local ring whose maximal ideal is the kernel of Λ(G) → F_p (reduction of the augmentation), and its open ideals form a basis of neighbourhoods of 0; likewise Ω(G) with maximal ideal the augmentation ideal. For G compact p-adic analytic, Λ(G) and Ω(G) are semilocal, and local iff G is pro-p.
hypotheses: G pro-p for the first statement; compact p-adic analytic for the equivalence.
proofSteps: For G finite p-group, the augmentation ideal of F_p[G] is nilpotent, so 1 + (augmentation ideal) consists of units; pass to the limit: every element of Λ(G) with unit image in F_p is a unit (geometric series converge).
If G is not pro-p, some finite quotient G/U has order divisible by a prime ℓ ≠ p or is not a p-group, and F_p[G/U] has more than one simple module; Λ(G) is then not local.
Semilocal: Λ(G) is a crossed product of Λ(U) (U open normal pro-p) by a finite group, whose Jacobson radical contains that of Λ(U).
acceptance: CFKSV use this for J pro-p to apply Nakayama's lemma to Λ(J)-modules.
Test: Λ(ℤ/ℓ) = ℤ_p[ℤ/ℓ] for ℓ ≠ p splits as a product of local rings, not local.

nodes.title: Complete filtrations with noetherian graded ring
nodes.statement: For a complete separated nonnegative adic filtration with F¹R⊆Jac(R) and left/right noetherian associated graded ring, the Rees filtration is Zariskian and R is left/right noetherian. If gr R is a domain, R is a domain. If gr R has finite left/right global dimension, the filtered lifting theorem gives gldim R≤gldim gr R. For Auslander regularity use the additional filtered Ext comparison and the Auslander condition, rather than claiming it follows from noetherianity alone.
hypotheses: Complete separated descending adic filtration, with its usual exhaustive extension to integer degrees; F¹R⊆Jac(R).
Associated graded ring noetherian on both sides; homological conclusions require the respective graded hypotheses.
proofSteps: Lift a finite homogeneous generating set of each graded ideal by successive approximation, using completeness.
Use the Zariskian filtered resolution and filtered Ext comparison of Venjakob Theorems 3.19–3.21 for the global-dimension and Auslander clauses.
Do not infer primality in the absence of a suitable filtered primeness theorem; only the domain implication is used here.
acceptance: State both sides; Iwasawa algebras are noncommutative.

nodes.title: Nakayama's lemma for compact modules over Λ(J)
nodes.statement: Let J be a pro-p group, 𝔪_J the maximal ideal of Λ(J), and M a compact (Hausdorff, linearly topologised) Λ(J)-module, for instance a quotient of a finitely generated Λ(G)-module for J ≤ G closed. Then M is finitely generated over Λ(J) iff M/𝔪_J M is finite iff the coinvariants M_J are a finitely generated ℤ_p-module; and M = 0 iff M/𝔪_J M = 0.
hypotheses: Compactness of M is essential (ℚ_p as a Λ(ℤ_p)-module with trivial action has M/𝔪M = 0).
proofSteps: Lazard II.2.2.2: every neighbourhood of 0 in Λ(J) contains 𝔪_J^n for large n, so for compact M the submodules 𝔪_J^n M shrink to 0.
If P is compact with 𝔪_J P = P then P = 𝔪_J^n P for all n, hence P = 0.
Lift generators of M/𝔪_J M to x₁, …, x_r; N = Σ Λ(J)x_i is compact, hence closed, and P = M/N satisfies 𝔪_J P = P.
M_J/p M_J = M/𝔪_J M because 𝔪_J is generated by p and the augmentation ideal.

nodes.title: Ordered coordinates of a uniform group
nodes.statement: For uniform U of dimension d and an ordered minimal generating set (u₁,…,u_d), the map c:Z_p^d→U given by c(x)=u₁^{x₁}⋯u_d^{x_d} is a homeomorphism of spaces. Coordinate order is fixed. For every n≥0 it identifies p^n Z_p^d with U^{p^n}, and the resulting coordinate residues parameterize U/U^{p^n}; c is a group homomorphism only in the abelian case.
hypotheses: p prime; U uniform; an ordered minimal generating set is selected.
proofSteps: Use pro-p p-adic powers from ProfiniteArithmetic.
Successive approximation along the lower p-series gives existence and uniqueness of ordered digits; compactness and Hausdorffness give the homeomorphism.

Compare with the valuation-basis criterion of Schneider Proposition 26.5 and the power-subgroup calculation in Corollary 26.12. The equivalence for every minimal generating set uses the uniform-group supplier gap.
acceptance: For U=Z_p^2 with its standard additive generators, c is the identity and the level-n quotient has p^{2n} elements.
For U=1, the empty product identifies Z_p^0 with the one-point group.
In a nonabelian uniform semidirect product, c(x+y) differs from c(x)c(y) for suitable x,y; a group-equivalence implementation must fail.

nodes.title: Finite-rank p-valuations
nodes.statement: A p-valuation is ω:U→R∪{∞} with ω(x)=∞ iff x=1, ω(xy⁻¹)≥min(ω(x),ω(y)), ω([x,y])≥ω(x)+ω(y), ω(x)>1/(p−1) for x≠1, and ω(x^p)=ω(x)+1. The valuation topology is the given topology. nodes.title: Ordered Iwasawa series and rationalization
nodes.statement: Let U be uniform with ordered generators and O a complete finite-free Z_p coefficient DVR. For b_i=u_i−1, ordered summation identifies ∏_(α∈N^d) O with O[[U]] as topological O-modules: (c_α)↦Σ c_α b₁^{α₁}⋯b_d^{α_d}. The topology is the complete maximal-ideal topology. This is a power-series ring isomorphism when U is abelian; multiplication is ordered and noncommutative in general. With K=Frac(O), K⊗_O O[[U]] consists exactly of ordered K-coefficient series with a common bounded denominator, not all formal K-series.
hypotheses: p prime; U uniform of dimension d; O finite free over Z_p and complete; the unramified coefficient case is the directly checked Schneider statement.
proofSteps: Use the supplied finite-quotient completion and the ordered coordinate basis.
Prove finite-level ordered monomials give the compatible bases; complete to obtain existence and uniqueness of all coefficient families.

Tensor the product by the field by inverting a single uniformizer: each element admits one common denominator, giving the bounded-denominator criterion. For ramified O use the finite-free completed coefficient comparison.
acceptance: For U=Z_p, recover the supplied coordinate γ↦1+T, with b^n mapping to T^n.
For U=1 only the constant monomial remains; O[[1]]=O and rationalization is K.
The family c_n=π^(−n) is a formal K-series but has no common bounded denominator, hence is excluded from K⊗O[[Z_p]].
For noncommuting u₁,u₂, b₁b₂ and b₂b₁ need not have the same coefficients; the module equivalence cannot silently be a commutative ring equivalence.

nodes.title: The graded ring of Ω(G) for uniform G
nodes.statement: For uniform U of dimension d, Ω(U)=F_p[[U]] has augmentation ideal J, is J-adically complete, and gr_J Ω(U)≅F_p[X₁,…,X_d], with X_i the symbol of u_i−1 for an ordered basis. For Λ(U)=Z_p[[U]] with maximal ideal m=(p,u_i−1), the analogous gr_m Λ(U)≅F_p[X₀,…,X_d] is asserted here only if [U,U]⊆U^{p²} for odd p, or [U,U]⊆U⁴ for p=2. Weighted p-valuations give the general uniform case; an unweighted integral polynomial claim for every uniform U is false.

proofSteps: Use the ordered series target to identify the coefficient filtration and augmentation generators.
For Ω, powerfulness puts commutators above degree two and the graded ordered monomials give the polynomial basis.

nodes.title: Lazard's noetherian theorem
nodes.statement: For a compact p-adic analytic group G, Λ(G) = ℤ_p⟦G⟧ and Ω(G) = F_p⟦G⟧ are left and right noetherian complete semilocal rings; for G pro-p they are local (Lazard V.2.2.4). The same holds for O⟦G⟧ = O ⊗_{ℤ_p} Λ(G), O the integers of a finite extension of ℚ_p.
hypotheses: G compact p-adic analytic.
proofSteps: Choose an open normal extra-powerful subgroup by the compact analytic structure and apply the corrected integral graded theorem.
Transfer noetherianity from the graded ring using the complete filtration; pass to a finite crossed product for G.
For O finite free over Z_p, use completed coefficient comparison from PMIA L1 (the ordinary tensor suffices because O is finite free).
acceptance: CFKSV cite this as 'well known'; it is used for the ascending chain argument of Proposition 2.3.

nodes.title: Auslander regularity of Iwasawa algebras
nodes.statement: For compact p-adic analytic G without p-torsion, Λ=Z_p[[G]] is noetherian with finite global dimension and satisfies the two-sided Auslander condition: for every finitely generated left Λ-module M and every right submodule N⊆Ext^i_Λ(M,Λ), Ext^j_(Λ^op)(N,Λ)=0 for j<i, with the analogous opposite-ring statement. For uniform U, Ω(U) is Auslander regular of global dimension dim U. These hypotheses are the homological input required by Fu.
hypotheses: G compact p-adic analytic; no element of order p. For the Ω clause U is uniform.
proofSteps: Choose an open extra-powerful uniform subgroup with polynomial filtered algebra.
Apply the Zariskian filtered Ext transfer, including the graded Auslander condition.
Pass from the open subgroup to G by the finite crossed-product Ext comparison in Venjakob Theorem 3.26; retain absence of p-torsion at the finite-global-dimension step.
acceptance: G=Z_p^d has integral dimension d+1 and mod-p dimension d.

nodes.title: Finite global dimension without p-torsion
nodes.statement: Let G be compact p-adic analytic of dimension d with no element of order p. Then Λ(G)=Z_p[[G]] is Auslander regular on both sides and has global dimension d+1. In particular every finitely generated Λ(G)-module has a bounded resolution by finitely generated projectives. The same integral dimension statement for O[[G]], O a finite extension ring of integers, needs the finite coefficient comparison and the DVR coefficient form of the filtered argument. No finite-global-dimension assertion is made for a group containing p-torsion.
hypotheses: No element of order p is essential: ℤ_p[ℤ/p] has infinite global dimension.
proofSteps: cd_p(G) = d for G without p-torsion (Lazard V.2.2.3 for p-valued groups, Serre's theorem that cd_p is inherited by open subgroups when there is no p-torsion).

Brumer: for a pro-p (or virtually pro-p) group without p-torsion, gl.dim Λ(G) = cd_p(G) + 1 (minimal resolutions of ℤ_p over the local ring Λ(U), then Serre's theorem for the finite extension Λ(G) ⊃ Λ(U)).

nodes.title: Rational Iwasawa global dimension

This is the bounded-denominator rational Iwasawa algebra; it is not the localization at all nonzero elements or Fu’s microlocal completion. The integral dimension is d+1.

nodes.title: Lazard exterior cohomology of uniform groups
nodes.statement: For a finitely generated powerful torsion-free pro-p group U of dimension d, continuous cohomology with trivial coefficients is naturally the graded F_p-algebra H*(U,F_p)≅∧*_(F_p) H¹(U,F_p), where dim H¹=d. Equivalently this is the Yoneda Ext algebra of the trivial module over Ω(U) in the continuous/compact module comparison. In particular the cup-product generators have square zero, including at p=2, and dim H^i=binomial(d,i). At 2 powerful means [U,U]⊆U⁴.

Use the multiplicative comparison of Lazard V.2.5.7.1 to identify cup products with exterior products; dimensions alone do not prove the ring assertion.

nodes.title: Twisting modules by a representation
nodes.statement: Let G be compact p-adic analytic, O a finite-free Z_p coefficient DVR and ρ:G→GL_n(O) continuous. For a finitely generated compact Λ_O(G)-module N, its O-linear diagonal twist is tw_ρ(N)=N⊗_O O^n, with g(m⊗z)=gm⊗ρ(g)z. For a Λ(G)-module M, first form M_O=O⊗_(Z_p)M, then take this twist. It is exact, is functorial on equivariant O-linear maps and sends Λ_O(G)^m to a free Λ_O(G)-module of rank mn. The 𝔐_H(G) preservation statement belongs to NE.2/twist-preserves-MHG; no quotient G/H is needed just to define twisting.

nodes.title: Iwasawa group homology and diagonal twists
nodes.statement: For compact p-adic analytic G without p-torsion and A=Q_p⊗Z_p[[G]], define H_i(G,M)=Tor_i^A(Q_p,M) for a finitely generated left A-module, with Q_p a right module by augmentation. For an integral compact Λ-module use completed Tor in the compact module category. If W is a finite-dimensional continuous Q_p representation admitting a G-stable Z_p lattice, the diagonal action g(m⊗w)=gm⊗gw defines M⊗W as a finitely generated A-module. Then H_i(G,M⊗W) is finite dimensional over Q_p and is zero for i>dim G. Integral lattices and completed tensor products must be compared before using the rational Tor formula.
hypotheses: G compact p-adic analytic, without p-torsion; M finitely generated over A; W finite dimensional with a continuous G-action and stable integral lattice.
proofSteps: Import continuous cohomology/compact homology and the completed Shapiro comparison from SelmerIwasawaCohomology L0 and L3.
A stable lattice makes the diagonal action continuous; the inverse diagonal twist identifies a twisted free A-module with a free module of rank dim W.
Resolve M by finitely generated projectives of length ≤d and tensor with the augmentation module. Each resulting term is finite dimensional; finite resolution length gives vanishing above d.
Compare compact integral resolutions after inverting p to justify the rational Tor description.

For G=Z_p and trivial M=Q_p, the resolution A --(γ−1)→ A gives H₀=H₁=Q_p and higher homology zero.
For G=Z_p acting on a one-dimensional W with γ acting by a≠1, the same resolution has differential a−1, so H₀=H₁=0.
The free diagonal twist has H₀ dimension dim W and no positive homology; a twist that forgets the inverse action fails this comparison.

nodes.title: The canonical Ore set S
nodes.statement: Let G be a compact p-adic analytic group with a closed normal subgroup H such that G/H ≅ ℤ_p. The canonical set is S = {f ∈ Λ(G) : Λ(G)/Λ(G)f is finitely generated as a left Λ(H)-module}. With O-coefficients, S_O is defined in the same way with Λ_O(G), Λ_O(H).
hypotheses: No hypothesis of 'no element of order p' is needed for S itself; CFKSV assume it only for later sections.
Abstractly: for a ring A that is a left B-module through left multiplication, S = {f : A/Af finitely generated over B}.
proofSteps: Define S by the finiteness condition on the cyclic module Λ(G)/Λ(G)f.
By iwasawa-free-over-open-subgroup, H may be replaced by any open subgroup of H in the definition.
acceptance: For H = 1, G = Γ ≅ ℤ_p: Λ(Γ)/Λ(Γ)f is finitely generated over ℤ_p iff f ≠ 0 and p ∤ f (Weierstrass), so S = Λ(Γ) ∖ pΛ(Γ).
Never replace S by the set of all nonzero divisors: localisation at all nonzero elements is neither defined in general nor equal to Λ(G)_S.

nodes.title: A central copy of ℤ_p in G/J
nodes.statement: Let H ◁ G closed with G/H ≅ ℤ_p and J ≤ H open, normal in G. Then G/J contains a subgroup Π ≅ ℤ_p that is open, central, and maps isomorphically onto an open subgroup of Γ = G/H; hence Ω(Π) ≅ F_p⟦T⟧ is a discrete valuation ring in the centre of Ω(G/J), and Λ(Π) ≅ ℤ_p⟦T⟧.
hypotheses: J open in H (so H/J is finite) and normal in G.
proofSteps: Choose a pro-p Sylow subgroup of G/J mapping onto Γ. Since Z_p is the free pro-p group on one generator, lift its generator inside that pro-p group. Its procyclic closure maps isomorphically onto Γ (an infinite procyclic pro-p group is Z_p), giving the section G/J=(H/J)⋊Γ. An arbitrary lift can carry an extra finite prime-to-p component and is not sufficient.
⟨γ⟩̄ acts on the finite group H/J by conjugation through a finite quotient, so an open subgroup Π = ⟨γ^{p^k}⟩̄ acts trivially; Π commutes with H/J and with ⟨γ⟩̄, hence is central.
Ω(Π) ≅ F_p⟦T⟧ by the power-series coordinate of ProfiniteProPGroups Layer 9.
acceptance: Π is central in G/J, not in G.
Test: G = ℤ_p ⋊ ℤ_p acting by a unit u ≠ 1 with H = ℤ_p: Π = ⟨γ^{p^k}⟩ with u^{p^k} ≡ 1 mod |H/J|.
For C_ℓ×Z_p with ℓ≠p, a lift with nontrivial C_ℓ-coordinate need not have pro-p closure. The construction first chooses a pro-p lift.

nodes.title: The algebra V(G/J)
nodes.statement: With Π as in central-zp-subgroup and R(Π) = Frac Ω(Π) ≅ F_p((T)), put V(G/J) = R(Π) ⊗_{Ω(Π)} Ω(G/J). It is a finite-dimensional algebra over the central field R(Π); Ω(G/J) → V(G/J) is injective; and for x ∈ Ω(G/J), right multiplication by x on V(G/J) is injective iff surjective iff x is a unit of V(G/J), and the same holds on the left.
hypotheses: Ω(G/J) is a finite free Ω(Π)-module (iwasawa-free-over-open-subgroup), of rank [G/J : Π].
proofSteps: V(G/J) = R(Π)^{[G/J:Π]} as an R(Π)-vector space; left and right multiplications are R(Π)-linear because R(Π) is central.
Linear algebra: an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space is surjective.
If x z = 1 in V then z x = 1 (finite-dimensional algebra), which gives the left–right symmetry used in Lemma 2.2.
acceptance: V(G/J) is not a division ring in general (G/J may be nonabelian with zero divisors in Ω(G/J)).

nodes.title: Criteria for membership in S (left)
nodes.statement: Let J ≤ H be pro-p, open in H and normal in G, with φ_J : Λ(G) → Λ(G/J) and ψ_J : Λ(G) → Ω(G/J). For f ∈ Λ(G) the following are equivalent: (i) f ∈ S; (ii) Λ(G/J)/Λ(G/J)φ_J(f) is a finitely generated ℤ_p-module; (iii) Ω(G/J)/Ω(G/J)ψ_J(f) is finite; (iv) right multiplication by ψ_J(f) on Ω(G/J) is injective.
hypotheses: J pro-p, open in H, normal in G (such J exist and are cofinal).
proofSteps: For M = Λ(G)/Λ(G)f: M_J = Λ(G/J)/Λ(G/J)φ_J(f) and M/𝔪_J M = Ω(G/J)/Ω(G/J)ψ_J(f); (i) ⇔ (ii) ⇔ (iii) by compact-nakayama (with H replaced by J).
Ω(Π) is a DVR, so a finitely generated Ω(Π)-module is torsion iff finite; Ω(G/J)/Ω(G/J)ψ_J(f) is finite iff right multiplication by ψ_J(f) has finite kernel, iff it is injective on V(G/J).
Ω(G/J) has no nonzero finite submodule, so finite kernel means zero kernel.
acceptance: Test on H = 1, G = Γ, J = 1: (iii) says F_p⟦T⟧/(f̄) finite, i.e. f̄ ≠ 0.

sources.match: Lemma 2.1(iii).

nodes.title: Criteria for membership in S (right)
nodes.statement: With J as before, f ∈ S iff Λ(G)/fΛ(G) is finitely generated as a right Λ(H)-module, iff Λ(G/J)/φ_J(f)Λ(G/J) is a finitely generated ℤ_p-module, iff Ω(G/J)/ψ_J(f)Ω(G/J) is finite, iff left multiplication by ψ_J(f) on Ω(G/J) is injective. In particular S is the same set whether defined with left or right modules.
hypotheses: As in canonical-set-left-criteria.
proofSteps: f ∈ S iff α_J(f) = image of ψ_J(f) in V(G/J) has a left inverse, iff it has a right inverse (quotient-total-algebra), iff left multiplication by ψ_J(f) is injective.
Reverse the argument of canonical-set-left-criteria for right modules.
acceptance: This symmetry is what makes S both a left and a right Ore set.

sources.match: Lemma 2.2(iv).

nodes.title: S-torsion equals finite generation over Λ(H)
nodes.statement: A finitely generated left (or right) Λ(G)-module M is S-torsion (every x ∈ M is killed by some s ∈ S) iff M is finitely generated over Λ(H).
hypotheses: G compact p-adic analytic, H ◁ G closed, G/H ≅ ℤ_p.
proofSteps: S-torsion ⇒ finitely generated: M is a quotient of ⊕ Λ(G)/Λ(G)f_i with f_i ∈ S, each finitely generated over Λ(H).

Conversely fix x ∈ M, J and Π as above, τ ∈ Λ(G) lifting T; the Λ(J)-submodules U_n = Σ_{k≤n} Λ(J)τ^k x of the finitely generated Λ(J)-module M stabilise (Λ(J) noetherian), giving s_n = τ^n − a_{n−1}τ^{n−1} − … − a₀ with s_n x = 0.
ψ_J(s_n) is a nonzero element of Ω(Π) (its image mod the augmentation of J is T^n + …), so right multiplication by it is injective on Ω(G/J), and s_n ∈ S by canonical-set-left-criteria (iv).
acceptance: The abstract direction (S-torsion ⇒ finitely generated over B) holds for any pair (A, B); the converse is the group-theoretic input.

nodes.title: The canonical Ore set theorem
nodes.statement: S is multiplicatively closed, a left and right Ore set in Λ(G) (for s ∈ S, r ∈ Λ(G) there are t₁, t₂ ∈ S and w₁, w₂ with s w₁ = r t₁ and w₂ s = t₂ r), and consists of nonzero divisors. Hence Mathlib's OreSet structure exists on S, on either side.
hypotheses: G compact p-adic analytic, H ◁ G closed, G/H ≅ ℤ_p.
proofSteps: Multiplicative: 0 → Λs₂/Λs₁s₂ → Λ/Λs₁s₂ → Λ/Λs₂ → 0 with the first term a quotient of Λ/Λs₁.
Ore: Λ/Λf and Λ/fΛ are finitely generated over Λ(H), hence S-torsion (Proposition 2.3): s x ∈ Λf and x s′ ∈ fΛ.
Nonzero divisors: φ_J(f) is not a zero divisor in Λ(G/J) for every J (criteria (iv) of Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 lifted from Ω to Λ), and Λ(G) = lim_J Λ(G/J).
Mathlib's OreSet needs the left Ore condition in the form t r = w s and right cancellation, which follows from S consisting of nonzero divisors.
acceptance: The scope is the source’s Z_p quotient, not the arbitrary-normal-subgroup generalization.
p ∉ S always: Λ(G)/pΛ(G) = Ω(G) is not finitely generated over Λ(H) because Γ = G/H is infinite; keep S and S* distinct.

nodes.title: Nilpotent kernels between finite levels
nodes.statement: For pro-p subgroups J ⊆ J′ of H, open in H and normal in G, the kernel K of Ω(G/J) → Ω(G/J′) is a nilpotent two-sided ideal: K = Ω(G/J) I_Δ with Δ = J′/J a finite p-group and I_Δ^n = 0.
hypotheses: J ⊆ J′ as stated.
proofSteps: K is generated by δ − 1 for δ ∈ Δ; Δ is normal so K = Ω(G/J) I_Δ = I_Δ Ω(G/J).
The augmentation ideal of F_p[Δ] is nilpotent for a finite p-group Δ, so K^n = Ω(G/J) I_Δ^n = 0.
acceptance: Test: G = Γ × ℤ/p, J = 1, J′ = ℤ/p: K = (σ − 1) with (σ − 1)^p = 0.

nodes.title: S as the elements regular modulo the prime radical
nodes.statement: Let 𝒩 be the preimage in Λ(G) of the prime radical of Ω(G/J) (independent of J by nilpotent-transition-kernel). Then S is the set of elements of Λ(G) that are regular (nonzero divisors) modulo 𝒩.
hypotheses: The prime radical of a noetherian ring is nilpotent and contains every nilpotent ideal.
The prime radical is the intersection of two-sided prime ideals, not Mathlib’s commutative nilradical; its nilpotence and semiprime Goldie quotient are explicit missing noncommutative inputs.
proofSteps: Λ(G)/𝒩 = Ω(G/J)/𝒩(Ω(G/J)); f is regular modulo 𝒩 iff α_J(f) is a unit of V(G/J)/𝒩(V(G/J)).
Units modulo nilpotent ideals are units, so this holds iff ψ_J(f) is a nonzero divisor in Ω(G/J), iff f ∈ S by Lemmas 2.1(iv) and 2.2(iv).
acceptance: This characterisation (due to Schneider) shows S is intrinsic in Λ(G) and H.

sources.match: Proposition 2.6.

nodes.title: The saturated Ore set S*
nodes.statement: S* = ⋃_{n≥0} p^n S. It is a multiplicatively closed left and right Ore set of nonzero divisors, and Λ(G)_{S*} = Λ(G)_S[1/p]. A finitely generated Λ(G)-module M is S*-torsion iff M/M(p) is finitely generated over Λ(H), where M(p) is the p-power torsion.
hypotheses: p is central in Λ(G).
proofSteps: p central and a nonzero divisor, so {p^n} is a central Ore set; products of Ore sets with a central Ore set are Ore.
Λ(G)_{S*} is the localisation of Λ(G)_S at p.
M/M(p) finitely generated over Λ(H) iff it is S-torsion (Proposition 2.3), iff M is S*-torsion.
acceptance: p ∉ S (Γ is infinite), so S* ≠ S.

nodes.title: The canonical localisation Λ(G)_S
nodes.statement: Λ(G)_S is Mathlib's Ore localisation of Λ(G) at the Ore set S (on the left; the right localisation is canonically isomorphic because S is two-sided Ore). The map Λ(G) → Λ(G)_S is injective, every s ∈ S becomes a unit, and any ring map Λ(G) → T inverting S factors uniquely through Λ(G)_S. Likewise Λ(G)_{S*}, O-coefficients included.

proofSteps: Instantiate OreLocalization with the OreSet structure of canonical-ore-theorem.
Injectivity: numeratorHom_inj, since S consists of (left) nonzero divisors.
Universal property: universalHom and universalHom_unique.
Left and right localisations agree: both satisfy the universal property for maps inverting S.

nodes.title: Ore localisation is flat
nodes.statement: For a left Ore set S of a ring R, the localisation R_S = S⁻¹R is flat as a right R-module, R_S ⊗_R M ≅ S⁻¹M naturally, and the kernel of M → R_S ⊗_R M is the S-torsion submodule of M. Hence a complex C of R-modules has R_S ⊗_R C acyclic iff every H^i(C) is S-torsion.
hypotheses: S left Ore; for the last statement C is bounded above with flat or projective terms, or any complex since R_S is flat.
proofSteps: S⁻¹M (Mathlib's OreLocalization of a module) is exact in M: a fraction m/s vanishes iff t m = 0 for some t ∈ S.
The natural map R_S ⊗_R M → S⁻¹M is an isomorphism (both are left adjoint-like; check on free modules and use right exactness).

Exactness of left fractions gives flatness of the (R_S,R)-bimodule and commutation with cohomology. This is a noncommutative bimodule assertion; pinned Module.Flat only covers commutative scalars and cannot supply it.
acceptance: CFKSV use exactness of localisation at S (p. 192).

nodes.title: The category 𝔐_H(G)
nodes.statement: 𝔐_H(G) is the full subcategory of finitely generated left Λ(G)-modules that are S*-torsion; equivalently those M with M/M(p) finitely generated over Λ(H). It is a Serre subcategory (closed under submodules, quotients and extensions). For H = 1, G = Γ it is the category of finitely generated torsion Λ(Γ)-modules.
hypotheses: G, H as in canonical-ore-set.
proofSteps: Closure under submodules uses that Λ(G) is noetherian (submodules of finitely generated modules are finitely generated); quotients and extensions are immediate from the torsion description.
For H = 1: S* = Λ(Γ) ∖ {0}, so S*-torsion means torsion.

nodes.title: Perfect complexes acyclic after localisation
nodes.statement: For a left denominator (Ore) set S of a ring R, Σ_S is the full subcategory of the category C^p(R) of perfect complexes of R-modules consisting of the C with R_S ⊗_R C acyclic. Σ_S contains 0, is closed under quasi-isomorphism, shifts and extensions; by ore-localization-flat, C ∈ Σ_S iff every H^i(C) is S-torsion. For R = Λ(G) and S = S*, a module in 𝔐_H(G) of finite projective dimension, viewed as a complex, lies in Σ_{S*}.
hypotheses: C^p(R): bounded complexes of finitely generated projective R-modules, up to quasi-isomorphism (GeneralAlgebraicKTheory K.4).
proofSteps: Define Σ_S by the acyclicity condition; check (i) 0 ∈ Σ_S, (ii) quasi-isomorphism invariance (R_S ⊗ − preserves quasi-isomorphisms of perfect complexes), (iii) shifts, (iv) extensions (long exact sequence after the exact functor R_S ⊗ −).
The cohomological description follows from flatness.
acceptance: Burns–Venjakob need a weaker condition (iv′) for subcategories not closed under extensions; Σ_S itself satisfies (iv).

nodes.title: K₀ is insensitive to complete ideals
nodes.statement: If I is a two-sided ideal of R and R is I-adically complete and separated and I⊆Jac(R), then K₀(R) → K₀(R/I) is an isomorphism; in particular K₀(Λ(G)) ≅ K₀(Ω(G)) ≅ K₀(F_p[G/U]) ≅ K₀(F_p[G/U]/Jac) for U open normal pro-p.
hypotheses: I-adic completeness and separatedness; I a two-sided ideal contained in Jac(R). For the displayed specializations, identify the appropriate complete ideals before applying the theorem.
proofSteps: Surjectivity: idempotent matrices lift modulo I (completeness).

Injectivity: lift stable isomorphisms between reductions of finite projectives, not merely projectives reducing to free modules. Lift the corresponding inverse maps; their composites are congruent to the identity modulo I and hence invertible by the complete geometric series. Thus isomorphism classes and stable relations lift. This is the outstanding K.3 extension request.
acceptance: Test: R = ℤ_p, I = pℤ_p: K₀(ℤ_p) = ℤ = K₀(F_p).

nodes.title: K₀(Λ(G)) injects into K₀ of a finite level
nodes.statement: For P an open normal pro-p subgroup of G, K₀(Λ(G)) → K₀(ℤ_p[G/P]) is injective.

proofSteps: Lift a ℤ_p[Δ]-isomorphism M/IM ⊕ ℤ_p[Δ]^r ≅ N/IN ⊕ ℤ_p[Δ]^r to β : M ⊕ Λ^r → N ⊕ Λ^r (M projective).
coker(β)_P = 0 gives coker β = 0 by Nakayama; H₁(P, N ⊕ Λ^r) = 0 gives ker(β)_P = 0, hence ker β = 0.

nodes.title: Detecting K₀(Λ(G)) by characters of a finite quotient
nodes.statement: With Δ = G/P and L ⊃ ℚ_p splitting ℚ̄_p[Δ], the composite λ : K₀(Λ(G)) → K₀(ℤ_p[Δ]) → K₀(ℚ_p[Δ]) → K₀(L[Δ]) ≅ ⊕_{ρ ∈ Irr(Δ)} K₀(L) ≅ ⊕_ρ ℤ is injective, and λ([M]) = ⊕_ρ j(τ[tw_ρ(M)]) with τ[U] = Σ_i (−1)^i [H_i(G, U)] for finitely generated M (finite global dimension).
hypotheses: Uses the Cartan–Brauer injectivity K₀(ℤ_p[Δ]) → K₀(ℚ_p[Δ]) and K₀(ℚ_p[Δ]) → K₀(L[Δ]) (Serre, Linear representations, 16 Theorem 34 Cor. 2 and 14.6; not freely available).
proofSteps: Compose the four maps; λ₁ is injective by k0-finite-level-injective, λ₂, λ₃ by the representation theory of finite groups, λ₄ is an isomorphism (Wedderburn and Morita).
Compute τ on modules through a finite projective resolution: τ[U] = Σ(−1)^i[Tor_i^{Λ(G)}(𝒪, U)] = Σ(−1)^i[H_i(G, U)], and similarly ε with Λ(Γ) and H_i(H, −).
acceptance: The Euler-characteristic formula needs finite global dimension (no element of order p).

nodes.title: H-homology of modules in 𝔐_H(G)
nodes.statement: For M ∈ 𝔐_H(G) the homology groups H_i(H, M) = Tor_i^{Λ(G)}(Λ(Γ), M) are finitely generated torsion Λ(Γ)-modules for all i ≥ 0, and vanish for i ≥ d if G has no element of order p.
hypotheses: cd_p(H) = d − 1 when H has no p-torsion.
proofSteps: Finite generation over Λ(Γ): Tor over Λ(G) of finitely generated modules.
M(p) is killed by p^t, so H_i(H, M(p)) is torsion; M_f = M/M(p) is finitely generated over Λ(H), so H_i(H, M_f) is a finitely generated ℤ_p-module, hence torsion over Λ(Γ); long exact sequence.
acceptance: Test: G = Γ, H = 1: H₀(1, M) = M is a torsion Λ(Γ)-module and higher homology vanishes.

hypotheses: 𝒪 finite free over ℤ_p.
proofSteps: M ⊗ 𝒪 ∈ 𝔐_H(G); tw_ρ of the p-power torsion is killed by the same power of p.
tw_{ρ|H}(Λ(H)^m) is free of finite rank over Λ(H), so tw_ρ(M_f) is finitely generated over Λ(H).

For G = ℤ_p² with H one factor, Λ(G)_{S*} = ℤ_p[[U, V]]_{(p,U)}[1/p] has infinitely many maximal ideals.
hypotheses: G, H as in NE.1.

For x = s⁻¹θ with θ ∈ ker ψ_J, s − θ ∈ S, so 1 − x = s⁻¹(s − θ) is a unit: ker ⊂ Jac.

nodes.title: The localized K₁ of Fukaya and Kato
nodes.statement: For a full subcategory Σ of C^p(R) containing 0 and closed under quasi-isomorphism, shifts and direct sums ((i)–(iii), (iv′)), K_1(R, Σ) is the abelian group generated by symbols [C, a] with C ∈ Σ and a : 1_R → d_R(C), subject to [0, id] = 1, [C′, d_R(f)∘a] = [C, a] for quasi-isomorphisms f, [C, a] = [C′, a′][C″, a″] for short exact sequences in Σ, and [C[1], a^{−1}] = [C, a]^{−1} (Definition 2.5, after Fukaya–Kato). For a left denominator set S and Σ_S the complexes with R_S ⊗ C acyclic, [C, a] ↦ θ_{C,a} (the composite 1 → d(R_S ⊗ C) → 1) is an isomorphism ch_{R,Σ_S} : K_1(R, Σ_S) ≅ K_1(R_S) (Fukaya–Kato Proposition 1.3.7), and any Σ ⊆ Σ_S gives ch_{R,Σ} : K_1(R, Σ) → K_1(R_S).
hypotheses: R a ring; S a left denominator set; Σ as stated. When Σ satisfies (iv) (closure under extensions) the definition is Fukaya–Kato's.
proofSteps: Relation (3) follows from (0)–(2) (Remark 2.6).
ch_{R,Σ_S} is well defined because each relation is respected by base change to R_S and acyclicity; it is bijective by Fukaya–Kato Proposition 1.3.7 (see the gap on Fukaya–Kato).
acceptance: This supplies the NE.2 remaining item "the Fukaya–Kato localized K_1(R, Σ_S) ≅ K_1(R_S)"; the proof of bijectivity is cited to Fukaya–Kato.
For Σ_{A·} use the smallest subcategory with (i)–(iii) and (iv′) containing A·: the extension-closed version need not lie in Σ^{ss} (finding E11).

sources.match: Definition 2.5 (Fukaya–Kato, weakened to (iv′)), Remark 2.6 and the isomorphism ch_{R,Σ_S}.

nodes.title: Relative classes of torsion perfect complexes
nodes.statement: For a regular two-sided Ore localization Λ→Λ_S, K₀(Λ,Λ_S) is represented by triples (P,α,Q), with finitely generated projectives P,Q and α:Λ_S⊗P≅Λ_S⊗Q, modulo stabilization, direct-sum and composition relations. Equivalently it is K₀ of perfect complexes acyclic over Λ_S. Fix ∂[s]=[Λ/Λs] for a regular denominator s. For a perfect torsion C set [C]=Σ_i(−1)^i[H^i(C)] whenever the cohomology modules have finite projective resolutions. Cone triangles obey [Cone(f)]=[D]−[C] for f:C→D. Burns–Venjakob’s characteristic map uses ∂ch(C,a)=−[C].
hypotheses: Λ noetherian; S a regular two-sided Ore set. For the displayed cohomology sum, each H^i(C) has a finite projective resolution.
proofSteps: Import relative K-theory and the perfect fibre comparison from GeneralAlgebraicKTheory K.4–K.5.
Send a relative triple to its localized acyclic comparison complex and check the relations; clear denominators for the inverse.
Fix signs on the one-term torsion module and its two-term resolution; transport additivity and shift through this comparison.
acceptance: For C=[Λ --T→ Λ] in degrees −1,0, [C]=[Λ/T], ∂[T]=[C], and ch(C)=T⁻¹.
Shifting C once negates its relative class and inverts ch(C), detecting the boundary convention.
For f:C→D, the cone has [Cone(f)]=[D]−[C]; the identity cone has zero class.
For Λ=Z_p[C_p][[T]], the perfect complex [Λ --T→ Λ] is admitted even though the trivial F_p-module has no finite projective resolution.

nodes.title: The localisation sequence for the canonical Ore set
nodes.statement: For Λ=Z_p[[G]] and the regular two-sided canonical denominator set S (or S*), the perfect-complex localization theorem gives K₁(Λ)→K₁(Λ_S)→∂K₀(Λ,Λ_S)→K₀(Λ)→K₀(Λ_S). The relative group is modeled by S-acyclic perfect complexes. If G has no p-torsion, finite global dimension identifies it with K₀ of finitely generated S-torsion modules, or with K₀(𝔐_H(G)) for S*. The module identification requires that extra hypothesis; the relative-perfect sequence does not.
hypotheses: G compact p-adic analytic; H closed normal with G/H≅Z_p; canonical regular Ore set S or its p-saturation.
Absence of p-torsion is assumed only for replacing relative perfect classes by all finitely generated torsion modules.
proofSteps: Apply the Waldhausen localization/fibration comparison to bounded projective complexes and its S-acyclic subcategory; identify π₀ of the fibre with relative triples.
With no p-torsion, use the resolution theorem and noetherian finite global dimension to compare torsion complexes with the Grothendieck group of torsion modules.
Do not use an abelian-category localization theorem as if it directly constructed the perfect-complex sequence.
acceptance: Keep the hypothesis 'no element of order p'; without it one works with perfect complexes (Σ_S*) instead of modules.

nodes.title: The boundary map ∂_G
nodes.statement: ∂_G : K₁(Λ(G)_{S*}) → K₀(𝔐_H(G)) is the connecting map of the localisation sequence, normalised so that for s ∈ S* (a nonzero divisor, unit in Λ(G)_{S*}), ∂_G([s]) = [Λ(G)/Λ(G)s] = [coker(x ↦ xs)]; it is a homomorphism. Naturality uses denominator-preserving ring maps and derived base change on perfect complexes; the module-valued comparison additionally needs the resolution identification on both sides.
hypotheses: The sign convention is the one of CFKSV §4 (∂(f(a)) = [Coker α] for right multiplication α by a).
proofSteps: For a matrix A ∈ GL_n(Λ_{S*}) ∩ M_n(Λ) acting by right multiplication on Λⁿ, ∂_G[A] = [coker A] (Swan's description).

Clear Ore denominators to express a general K₁ class as a quotient of classes of integral matrices invertible after localization. The boundary is the difference of their cokernel classes. Multiplication by a noncentral denominator must respect the chosen left-module/right-matrix convention; a single integral matrix modulo integral units does not represent every class.
acceptance: Fix the sign: ∂[s] = +[Λ/Λs]; the opposite convention changes characteristic elements to their inverses.

nodes.title: Surjectivity of ∂_G
nodes.statement: If G has no element of order p, then ∂_G : K₁(Λ(G)_{S*}) → K₀(𝔐_H(G)) is surjective; equivalently every M ∈ 𝔐_H(G) has [M] = 0 in K₀(Λ(G)).
hypotheses: No element of order p.
proofSteps: By exactness, surjectivity of ∂_G is equivalent to [M] ↦ 0 in K₀(Λ(G)).
For each ρ ∈ Irr(Δ): H_i(H, tw_ρ M) is Λ_𝒪(Γ)-torsion, so ε[tw_ρ M] = 0 in K₀(Λ_𝒪(Γ)) ≅ ℤ (rank), hence τ = 0.
λ[M] = ⊕ j(τ[tw_ρ M]) = 0 and λ is injective.
acceptance: For G = Γ this is the statement that finitely generated torsion Λ(Γ)-modules have zero class in K₀(Λ(Γ)) = ℤ.

nodes.title: Characteristic elements
nodes.statement: For M ∈ 𝔐_H(G) (G without element of order p), a characteristic element of M is any ξ_M ∈ K₁(Λ(G)_{S*}) with ∂_G(ξ_M) = [M]. Characteristic elements exist (boundary-surjective) and two of them differ by an element of the image of K₁(Λ(G)) → K₁(Λ(G)_{S*}).
hypotheses: A characteristic element is a lift of a class, not a canonical scalar; its ambiguity is exactly the image of K₁(Λ(G)).
proofSteps: Existence by surjectivity of ∂_G; ambiguity by exactness at K₁(Λ(G)_{S*}).
acceptance: Recover the characteristic power series up to Λ(Γ)^× for G = Γ (commutative-cyclic-comparison).

nodes.statement: For G = Γ ≅ ℤ_p and H = 1: S* = Λ(Γ) ∖ {0}, Λ(Γ)_{S*} = Q(Γ) is the fraction field, K₁(Q(Γ)) = Q(Γ)^×, K₀(𝔐_H(G)) is the Grothendieck group of finitely generated torsion Λ(Γ)-modules, and ∂ sends f/g to [Λ/f] − [Λ/g]. A characteristic element of a torsion module M is its characteristic power series char(M) (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras L4) up to Λ(Γ)^×.
hypotheses: Λ(Γ) ≅ ℤ_p[[T]] is a regular local ring of dimension 2; K₁(Λ(Γ)) = Λ(Γ)^×.
proofSteps: Q(Γ) is a field, so K₁ = units by the determinant.
For M ≅ ⊕Λ/(f_i) up to pseudo-isomorphism, [M] = Σ[Λ/f_i]: a pseudo-null (finite) module has class 0 in K₀(𝔐), e.g. 0 → Λ/p →^T Λ/p → F_p → 0 gives [F_p] = 0; then ∂(∏ f_i) = [M].
acceptance: The ambiguity K₁(Λ(Γ)) = Λ(Γ)^× is exactly 'up to units'.
Check a pseudo-null (finite) module: its characteristic element is a unit.

nodes.title: Surjectivity of ∂ for every compact p-adic Lie group
nodes.statement: Let G be a compact p-adic Lie group with closed normal H and G/H ≅ ℤ_p, possibly with elements of order p. In the localisation sequence K₁(Λ(G)) → K₁(Λ(G)_S) → K₀(Λ(G), Λ(G)_S) → K₀(Λ(G)) → K₀(Λ(G)_S), the boundary map ∂ is surjective: the map η : K₀(Λ(G), Λ(G)_S) → K₀(Λ(G)) is zero.
hypotheses: No hypothesis on p-torsion in G (CFKSV assume none; see boundary-surjective).
proofSteps: Use Kakde Lemma 5’s injective representation map λ:K₀(Λ)→∏_ρK₀(L), with ρ factoring through a finite quotient by an open normal pro-p subgroup.

Represent a relative class by a bounded perfect S-acyclic complex C. Twist its finite projective complex by each ρ and derive H-coinvariants. After the Γ fraction-field localization the complex is acyclic; its Euler rank over O[[Γ]] is therefore zero.
Apply derived augmentation to obtain zero Euler rank over O, hence λ(η[C])=0. Injectivity implies η[C]=0 and exactness gives surjectivity of ∂.

A relative triple involves finite projective terms and a localized isomorphism, so its perfect-complex argument applies even with p-torsion. If using an integral left-linear map a:P→Q with localized isomorphism, its kernel is S-torsion and P is S-torsion-free, hence a is injective. Q’s torsion-freeness alone would not prove this. No arbitrary scalar clearing of noncentral left denominators is asserted.
acceptance: For G=C_p×Z_p, the relative boundary is still surjective although the ring does not have finite global dimension.
A relative triple has projective terms and a localized isomorphism; clearing denominators gives a perfect cokernel, not a resolution theorem for arbitrary modules.

sources.match: Lemma 5 and its proof (pp. 8–9).

nodes.title: The ring homomorphism Φ_ρ : Λ(G) → M_n(Λ_𝒪(Γ))
nodes.statement: G is a compact p-adic Lie group with a closed normal H and G/H = Γ ≅ ℤ_p (topological generator fixed, Λ(Γ) = ℤ_p[[T]]), 𝒪 the ring of integers of a finite extension L of ℚ_p, Λ_𝒪(Γ) = 𝒪[[T]] with fraction field Q_𝒪(Γ), and ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) continuous. By continuity ρ gives ρ : Λ(G) → M_n(𝒪) (14). The continuous homomorphism G → (M_n(𝒪) ⊗_{ℤ_p} Λ(Γ))^×, σ ↦ ρ(σ) ⊗ σ̄ (σ̄ the image of σ in Γ) (16), extends to a ring homomorphism Φ_ρ : Λ(G) → M_n(Λ_𝒪(Γ)) (15), with Φ_ρ(p) = pI_n; composing with the augmentation Λ_𝒪(Γ) → 𝒪 gives (14).
proofSteps: M_n(𝒪) ⊗_{ℤ_p} Λ(Γ) = M_n(Λ_𝒪(Γ)) because 𝒪 is free of finite rank over ℤ_p.
The map on G is a continuous homomorphism into the units of a compact ring, so it extends to the completed group algebra (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras L1).
acceptance: Φ_ρ records the Γ-component σ̄ as well as ρ(σ); for H = 1 and ρ trivial it is the identity of Λ(Γ).

nodes.title: Φ_ρ extends to the localisation at S*
nodes.statement: (Lemma 3.3.) Φ_ρ extends to a ring homomorphism Φ_ρ : Λ(G)_{S*} → M_n(Q_𝒪(Γ)) (17): Φ_ρ(s) is invertible for every s ∈ S* = ∪_n pⁿS.
hypotheses: S the canonical Ore set of NE.1.
proofSteps: It suffices that the reduction Φ̃_ρ(s) ∈ M_n(k[[T]]) has nonzero determinant for s ∈ S.
Φ̃_ρ factors through δ : Ω(G/J) → M_n(k[[T]]) for a pro-p open J ⊆ H normal in G inside ker ρ̃ (GL_n(k) is finite).
A central Π ≅ ℤ_p of G/J inside ker ρ̃ has δ(Ω(Π)) ⊆ k[[T]]I_n, and Q(k[[T]]) is finite over R(Π); δ extends to R(Π) ⊗_{Ω(Π)} Ω(G/J), where ψ_J(s) is a unit (NE.1), so δ(ψ_J(s)) is invertible.
acceptance: The extension is to matrices over the fraction field Q_𝒪(Γ), not over Λ_𝒪(Γ): elements of S become invertible only after inverting nonzero power series.

nodes.title: Akashi series
nodes.statement: Assume G has no element of order p, let H◁G with G/H=Γ, and let M∈𝔐_H(G). Then H_i(H,M) are finitely generated torsion Λ(Γ)-modules and vanish above cd_p H. With f_(i,M) their characteristic series, the finite alternating product Ak(M)=∏_i f_(i,M)^{(−1)^i} modulo Λ(Γ)^× defines Ak:K₀(𝔐_H(G))→Q(Γ)^×/Λ(Γ)^×. For O-coefficient M use Λ_O(Γ); its coefficient norm satisfies N(Ak_O(M))=Ak(M). A particular bounded-homology perfect variant may be defined separately, but there is no infinite product for arbitrary p-torsion G.
hypotheses: G has no element of order p, ensuring a bounded homology product. Alternatively specify a category on which H-homology is bounded and the exact-sequence operations preserve that bound.
proofSteps: H_i(H, M) = Tor_i^{Λ(G)}(Λ(Γ), M) is finitely generated over Λ(Γ); torsion because H_i(H, M(p)) is killed by a power of p and H_i(H, M/M(p)) is finitely generated over ℤ_p.
Additivity on short exact sequences from the long exact sequence of H-homology and multiplicativity of characteristic series.
(40): N(g_i) = f_i mod Λ(Γ)^× (Bourbaki, Commutative Algebra VII §4.8, Prop. 18; PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras L4).
acceptance: Ak is defined only modulo units; the Euler-characteristic formula uses its value at T = 0 up to p-adic units.

nodes.title: The evaluation–Akashi diagram
nodes.statement: (Lemma 3.7.) With Δ_ρ([M]) = Ak_𝒪(tw_{ρ̂}(M)) (41)–(42), where ρ̂(g) = ρ(g^{−1})^t is the contragredient, and ∂_Γ : Q_𝒪(Γ)^× → Q_𝒪(Γ)^×/Λ_𝒪(Γ)^×, the square ∂_Γ ∘ Φ′_ρ = Δ_ρ ∘ ∂_G (43) commutes.
hypotheses: G without elements of order p (so ∂_G is defined on modules).
proofSteps: Functoriality of the localisation sequence with Morita equivalence gives (47): ∂_1 ∘ v_1 ∘ u_1 = v_0 ∘ u_0 ∘ ∂_G.

For a finite projective resolution P_• of M, u_0([M]) = Σ(−1)^i[M_n(Λ_𝒪(Γ)) ⊗_{Λ(G)} P_i] (49); the row-vector Morita functor identifies (Rⁿ)^t ⊗_{M_n(R)} M_n(R) ⊗_{Λ(G)} P_i with Λ_𝒪(Γ) ⊗_{Λ_𝒪(G)} tw_{ρ̂}(P_i) (50), since the right action (τ ⊗ x^t)g = τḡ ⊗ x^tρ(g) corresponds, after passing from right modules to left modules, to the contragredient ρ̂.
tw_{ρ̂}(P_•) resolves tw_{ρ̂}(M), and Λ_𝒪(Γ) ⊗ − computes H_i(H, tw_{ρ̂}(M)), whose alternating class is Ak_𝒪.
acceptance: The contragredient ρ̂ appears on the module side: the evaluation at ρ corresponds to twisting by ρ̂.
The row action is multiplication by ρ(g), so (v·g)·h=v·(gh). Multiplying rows by ρ(g)^t would reverse the order for noncommuting matrices.

nodes.title: Characteristic elements compute twisted Euler characteristics
nodes.statement: (Theorem 3.6.) Assume G has no element of order p. Let M ∈ 𝔐_H(G) with characteristic element ξ_M. For every continuous ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) with χ(G, tw_{ρ̂}(M)) finite, ξ_M(ρ) ≠ 0, ∞ and χ(G, tw_{ρ̂}(M)) = |ξ_M(ρ)|_p^{−m_ρ}, where m_ρ = [L : ℚ_p] and |p|_p = 1/p.
hypotheses: G has no element of order p; χ(G, tw_{ρ̂}(M)) finite.
proofSteps: If χ(G, W) is finite (W = tw_{ρ̂}(M)), then φ(f_{i,W}) ≠ 0 for all i, φ(Ak(W)) ≠ 0, ∞ and χ(G, W) = |φ(Ak(W))|_p^{−1} (44) (Coates–Schneider–Sujatha, via Hochschild–Serre and χ(Γ, N) = |f_N(0)|_p^{−1}; requested from SelmerIwasawaCohomology L3).
By (40) and N ∘ φ = φ ∘ N, χ(G, W) = |φ(Ak_𝒪(W))|_p^{−m_ρ} (45).
Lemma 3.7 gives ∂_Γ(Φ′_ρ(ξ_M)) = Ak_𝒪(tw_{ρ̂}(M)) (46), and the value at T = 0 is ξ_M(ρ).
acceptance: The formula determines |ξ_M(ρ)|_p only; the unit part of ξ_M(ρ) is not an Euler-characteristic invariant.

nodes.title: Evaluation at Artin representations under a finiteness condition
nodes.statement: (Theorem 3.8, Lemma 3.9.) Assume G has no element of order p and let M ∈ 𝔐_H(G) satisfy H_i(H′, M) finite for all i ≥ 1 and all open H′ ⊆ H normal in G (51). Then for every Artin representation ρ (ker ρ open), Ak_𝒪(tw_ρ(M)) ∈ Λ_𝒪(Γ)[1/p] modulo units (52), ξ_M(ρ) ≠ ∞, and ξ_M(ρ) ≠ 0 iff χ(G, tw_{ρ̂}(M)) is finite.
hypotheses: G without elements of order p; (51).
proofSteps: With H′ = ker ρ ∩ H, W = tw_ρ(M) is M_𝒪ⁿ as an H′-module, so H_i(H′, W) is finite for i ≥ 1 (54); Hochschild–Serre for Δ = H/H′ shows H_i(H, W) is killed by a power of p for i ≥ 1, so g_{i,W} = π^{μ_i} (53).
Hence Ak_𝒪(W) = g_{0,W}∏π^{(−1)^iμ_i} (56), and φ(Ak_𝒪(W)) ≠ 0 iff φ(g_{0,W}) ≠ 0 iff χ(G, W) is finite.
Lemma 3.7 then gives Φ′_ρ(ξ_M) ∈ Λ_𝒪(Γ)_𝔭 and the finiteness criterion.
acceptance: Condition (51) is on all open normal H′ ⊆ H; it holds for M iff it holds for M(p) and M/M(p).

nodes.title: Artin formalism for G-Euler characteristics
nodes.statement: (Theorem 3.10.) Let G be a compact p-adic Lie group without elements of order p (no H needed), G′ ⊆ G open normal, Δ = G/G′, V the irreducible Q̄_p-representations of Δ, all realised over L with integers 𝒪. For finitely generated M, χ(G′, M) is finite iff χ(G, tw_ρ(M)) is finite for all ρ ∈ V, and then χ(G′, M)^{[L:ℚ_p]} = ∏_{ρ∈V} χ(G, tw_ρ(M))^{n_ρ} (58).
hypotheses: G without elements of order p.
proofSteps: 0 → 𝒪[Δ] → ⊕_ρ L_ρ^{n_ρ} → W → 0 with W finite (59); tensor with a projective resolution P_• of M_𝒪 (61).
K_i = W ⊗ C_i is finite and [C] = 0 in K₀(𝒪[Δ]) (injectivity into K₀(L[Δ])), so ∏♯H_i(K)^{(−1)^i} = θ([C]) = 1 (67)–(69).
acceptance: The exponent [L : ℚ_p] on the left accounts for the 𝒪-coefficients.

For E = X₁(11), p = 5, F_∞ = ℚ(E_{5^∞}), G = Gal(F_∞/ℚ), H = Gal(F_∞/ℚ^cyc), M = X(E/F_∞) ∈ 𝔐_H(G), and the degree-4 Artin representations ρ_i induced from nontrivial characters of Gal(F_i/ℚ(μ_5)) with F_1 = ℚ(E_5), F_2 = ℚ(E_{2,5}) (E_2 the conductor-11 curve with E_2(ℚ) = 0): χ(G, tw_{ρ_1}(M)) = 5³ and χ(G, tw_{ρ_2}(M)) = 5, so |ξ_{E,5}(ρ_1)|_5^{−1} = 5³ and |ξ_{E,5}(ρ_2)|_5^{−1} = 5 (ρ̂_i = ρ_i).

Likewise χ(G, tw_{ρ_2}X)⁴ = 5⁸/5⁴ = 5⁴.

nodes.title: The integrality conjecture for characteristic elements (Conjecture 4.8)
nodes.statement: Assume G has no element of order p. Put R₁ = Λ(G), R₂ = Λ(G)[1/p], R₃ = Λ(G)_{S*} (so R₁ ⊂ R₂ ⊂ R₃), A₁ = Λ_𝒪(Γ), A₂ = Λ_𝒪(Γ)[1/p], and α : R₃^× → K₁(R₃) the canonical map (surjective by NE.2/units-surject-k1). Let ℜ(G) be the continuous representations ρ of the form (11) (over the integers of finite extensions of ℚ_p) and 𝔄(G) ⊂ ℜ(G) the Artin ones. Conjecture 4.8 is the proposition that, for every ξ ∈ K₁(R₃), in each of four cases the assertions (a)–(d) are equivalent: Case 1: (a) ξ ∈ α(R₂ ∩ R₃^×), (b) ξ(ρ) ≠ ∞ for all ρ, (c) Φ′_ρ(ξ) ∈ A₂ for all ρ, (d) Φ′_ρ(ξ) ∈ A₂ for all Artin ρ; Case 2: α(R₁ ∩ R₃^×), ξ(ρ) finite and in 𝒪, Φ′_ρ(ξ) ∈ A₁; Case 3: α(R₂^×), ξ(ρ) ≠ 0, ∞, Φ′_ρ(ξ) ∈ A₂^×; Case 4: α(R₁^×), ξ(ρ) finite and in 𝒪^×, Φ′_ρ(ξ) ∈ A₁^×. (Lemma 4.9.) In each case (a) ⇒ (b), (b) ⇔ (c) and (c) ⇒ (d).
hypotheses: a conjecture: it is stated as a proposition, never assumed by a downstream theorem
CFKSV report it true for G = ℤ_p^d × Δ (Δ finite of order prime to p), proof omitted, and cite Kato [21] Proposition 8.19 as further evidence; neither is planned (recorded as remaining)
The supporting direct-product case and the cited Kato Proposition 8.19 still require their precise source proofs; they do not turn the general integrality conjecture into a theorem.
proofSteps: Lemma 4.9: (c) ⇒ (d) is trivial, (c) ⇒ (b) because ξ(ρ) is the image of Φ′_ρ(ξ) under augmentation; (a) ⇒ (b) since ξ = α(p^{−m}f) gives ξ(ρ) = p^{−mn} det ρ(f).

For (b)⇒(c), first prove on the defining group-element ring map (and hence on all matrix determinants) the exact identity Φ′_(ρη)(ξ)(T)=Φ′_ρ(ξ)(a(1+T)−1), a=η(γ). This uses Φ_ρ(g)=ρ(g)ḡ and does not pass through Akashi series modulo units. A pole at α in the maximal ideal is detected by the continuous character η(γ)=1+α. Weierstrass preparation then gives the pole criterion; the integral and unit cases also require their stated integral-value/nonvanishing conditions. CFKSV (94) has the inverse substitution under these conventions (E16).
acceptance: For G=Γ, Case 2 requires finite integral values at all admitted characters. Absence of poles alone tests Case 1, and is insufficient for Case 2: the constant p⁻¹ has no poles but is not integral. The function T/(T−p) has a pole detected at η(γ)=1+p.

nodes.title: SK₁ and the quotient K′₁ of Iwasawa algebras
nodes.statement: For a finite group P and 𝒪 the integers of a finite extension L/ℚ_p, SK₁(𝒪[P]) = ker(K₁(𝒪[P]) → K₁(L[P])). For a compact p-adic Lie group G, SK₁(Λ_𝒪(G)) := lim_U SK₁(𝒪[G/U]), and SK₁(Λ_𝒪(G)_S), SK₁(Λ̂_𝒪(G)_S) are its images in K₁(Λ_𝒪(G)_S) and K₁ of the p-adic completion Λ̂_𝒪(G)_S. K′₁(R) := K₁(R)/SK₁(R) for R each of these rings. Then K′₁(Λ_𝒪(G)) ≅ lim_Δ K′₁(𝒪[Δ]) over the finite quotients Δ of G, and K′₁(Λ(G)) ≅ lim_{Ḡ} K′₁(Λ(Ḡ)) over the quotients Ḡ = G/U by open pro-p subgroups U ≤ H normal in G.
hypotheses: G compact p-adic Lie.
proofSteps: K₁(Λ(G)) ≅ lim_n K₁(Λ(G)/J^n) for the Jacobson radical J (Fukaya–Kato, Proposition 1.5.1; see the gap on Fukaya–Kato).
For the finite groups K₁(Λ(G)/J^n, I_{Δ,n}/J^n) the limits over Δ and n commute, and ⋂_n⋂_Δ I_{Δ,n} = 0, so K₁(Λ_𝒪(G)) ≅ lim_Δ K₁(𝒪[Δ]) (Lemma 19).
Each SK₁(𝒪[Δ]) is finite (Wall; see the gap on Oliver's book), so the quotients pass to the limit.
Corollary 20 by cofinality of the finite quotients.
acceptance: K′₁ is used because SK₁ is invisible to Artin evaluations; uniqueness in the main conjecture holds in K′₁.

nodes.title: Semisimple total quotient in dimension one
nodes.statement: Suppose G is compact p-adic analytic with an open central Γ₀≅Z_p, and O is a finite extension ring of integers. With R=O[[Γ₀]] and F=Frac(R), define Q_O(G)=F⊗_R O[[G]]. It is the classical total ring of fractions and a finite-dimensional separable semisimple F-algebra; changing Γ₀ gives the canonically isomorphic total quotient. It is distinct from Λ(G)_S and Λ(G)[1/p].
hypotheses: G has an open central Z_p-subgroup (the one-dimensional situation of the cited routes); O finite over Z_p; coefficients are characteristic zero after tensoring.
proofSteps: The finite free Λ_O(Γ₀)-basis from open-subgroup freeness has multiplication given by a central finite-group cocycle; use the generic crossed/twisted algebra from InductionRestriction Layer 7. This argument does not depend on the later Kakde carry calculations.
After extending to an algebraic closure of F, the finite twisted group algebra is semisimple by averaging in characteristic zero.
Every regular element becomes an invertible endomorphism of the finite-dimensional semisimple algebra; use the universal localization property.
acceptance: For G=Z_p, Q_O(G)=Frac(O[[T]]), whereas the canonical S-localization still does not invert p.
For G=C₂×Z_p with p odd, Q_Zp(G) is the product of two copies of Frac(Z_p[[T]]); it is not a field.
For the trivial finite quotient, the construction is just the central field F; changing Γ₀ to Γ₀^p gives the same total quotient of the larger algebra.

nodes.title: Reduced norms and the surviving SK₁ ambiguity
nodes.statement: For the dimension-one total quotient Q=∏_i M_(n_i)(D_i), use the componentwise reduced norms supplied by IntegralHeckeAndGaloisDeterminants Layer 0. They induce Nrd:K₁(Q)→ζ(Q)^×, with kernel SK₁(Q). After a common splitting field, equality of determinant functions on all simple factors is equivalent to equality of reduced norms. Thus equality of all such characterwise determinants determines a localized class only modulo the inverse image of SK₁(Q); without injectivity K₁(Λ_S)→K₁(Q), it need not even determine a unique class modulo an internally defined kernel. Artin evaluations at admissible cyclotomic points require a separate separation argument. Kakde’s finite-level SK₁(Λ) and this SK₁(Q) are different definitions.
hypotheses: Dimension-one Q as above; all simple factors and their centers retained; a common splitting field.
For conclusions about Λ_S additionally state the kernel of its map to Q; equality at isolated points is not substituted for equality of determinant functions.
proofSteps: Import the reduced norm as the splitting-independent determinant law, extend to stable matrices and factor through K₁ using elementary matrices.
Read equality of split determinants componentwise; faithful extension of centers detects equality of the reduced norms.
Take the kernel of K₁(Λ_S)→K₁(Q)→ζ(Q)^× and retain it explicitly; use a proved power-series separation theorem only when converting interpolation values to functions.
acceptance: For Q=M₂(F), Nrd is the ordinary determinant, so diag(a,b) maps to ab, not (ab)².
For Q=F×F the two components remain ordered; (a,b) and (b,a) cannot be identified by multiplying them.
A hypothetical nontrivial x∈SK₁(Q) has every split determinant equal to 1 but x≠1; no proof of uniqueness can discard this possibility.

sources.match: Uses Det as the reduced-norm-valued character function; the main theorem is an existence assertion.
Makes the total quotient SK₁ obstruction explicit and reduces its vanishing conditionally.
Relates splitting determinants to reduced norms and explains why a Fitting equality cannot recover a relative boundary.

nodes.title: Functoriality and induction of Artin evaluation
nodes.statement: For the CFKSV twist Φ_ρ(g)=ρ(g)⊗ḡ and Artin representations admitting the localized map, coefficient extension carries its determinant to the extended determinant, Φ_(ρ⊕σ) gives the product of evaluations, and the trivial n-dimensional representation evaluates a scalar unit u as u^n. For an open subgroup U⊆G with compatible canonical denominator sets, the transfer in K₁ evaluates at σ as the original class at Ind_U^G σ. Quotient descent evaluates at a representation of G/N by inflation. All augmentation evaluations are asserted only on the regular-at-zero domain, with zeros/poles recorded separately.
hypotheses: Representations continuous with finite image on stable O-lattices; coefficient extension contains their values.
For transfer/quotient statements require the relevant ring maps or finite-projective restriction functors to carry the localized perfect subcategories to each other.
proofSteps: Compare the matrix twisting maps on group elements and use continuity of the coefficient extension.
Use block determinants for sums and the coset matrix for an induced representation; apply Morita invariance with the same left-module convention.
Transport through the Ore universal property when denominators are invertible; restrict augmentation to its domain of regularity.
acceptance: For a scalar unit u∈O^× and dim ρ=n, evaluation is u^n.
For G=C₂×Γ, U=Γ and σ=1, Ind σ=1⊕sgn; evaluation after transfer is the product of the two scalar evaluations.
A class represented by T has augmentation zero and T⁻¹ a pole; neither belongs to an everywhere O^×-valued evaluation map.

nodes.title: The dual Selmer module over the trivialising extension of E[p^∞]
nodes.statement: Let E/ℚ be an elliptic curve and p ≥ 5 a prime of good ordinary reduction ('our hypotheses on p'), F_∞ = ℚ(E_{p^∞}) ⊇ ℚ(μ_{p^∞}) ⊇ ℚ^cyc (Weil pairing), G = Gal(F_∞/ℚ) (a closed subgroup of GL₂(ℤ_p), of dimension 4 without CM and 2 with CM, and with no element of order p), H = Gal(F_∞/ℚ^cyc), Γ = Gal(ℚ^cyc/ℚ). For an algebraic extension L/ℚ the Selmer group is 𝒮(E/L) = ker(H¹(L, E_{p^∞}) → Π_w H¹(L_w, E(L̄_w))) over the non-archimedean w, and X(E/L) = Hom(𝒮(E/L), ℚ_p/ℤ_p); for L Galois over F, X(E/L) is a finitely generated left Λ(Gal(L/F))-module. Also G_F = Gal(F_∞/F), H_F = Gal(F_∞/F^cyc) and Y(E/K) = X(E/K)/X(E/K)(p).
hypotheses: p ≥ 5 and good ordinary reduction; p ≥ 5 is what rules out p-torsion in G ⊂ GL₂(ℤ_p)
This is the module-level Selmer instance; the separate equivariant-compact-support and dual-complex targets specify the complex-level objects.
proofSteps: Import the Selmer definition, local Kummer conditions and restriction maps from SelmerIwasawaCohomology L2; arithmetic duality is supplied by ArithmeticGaloisDuality.

For a compact pro-p open subgroup U of Gal(L/F), prove finiteness of the mod-p U-coinvariants using the appropriate Selmer restriction/control theorem, including its local error terms. Compact Nakayama then gives finite generation over Λ(U), and the open-index comparison gives it over Λ(Gal(L/F)). The required control theorem is a supplier gap; finite generation of X(E/F) alone is not the missing comparison.
acceptance: Check that for L = F finite X(E/F) is the usual Pontryagin dual of the p-primary Selmer group, with ℤ_p-corank the Mordell–Weil rank plus the corank of Ш[p^∞].

nodes.title: Criteria for X(E/F_∞) ∈ 𝔐_H(G) (Lemmas 5.3–5.4, Corollary 5.5, Proposition 5.6)
nodes.statement: (Lemma 5.3.) If X(E/F_∞) ∈ 𝔐_H(G), then for each finite F ⊂ F_∞: (i) X(E/F^cyc) is Λ(Γ_F)-torsion; (ii) H_i(H_F, X(E/F_∞)) = 0 for i ≥ 1; (iii) H_i(H_F, Y(E/F_∞)) is finite for i = 1, 2 and zero for i > 2; and μ_{G_L}(X(E/F_∞)) = μ_{Γ_L}(X(E/L^cyc)) when G_L is pro-p. (Lemma 5.4.) If X(E/F^cyc) is Λ(Γ_F)-torsion for all finite F and some L has G_L pro-p, μ_{G_L}(X(E/F_∞)) = μ_{Γ_L}(X(E/L^cyc)) and H₁(H_L, Y(E/F_∞)) finite, then X(E/F_∞) ∈ 𝔐_H(G). (Corollary 5.5.) If E has CM, X(E/F_∞) ∈ 𝔐_H(G) iff μ_{Γ_L}(X(E/L^cyc)) = 0 for some L with G_L pro-p. (Proposition 5.6.) If some L ⊂ F_∞ with G_L pro-p carries an elliptic curve E′ isogenous to E over L with X(E′/L^cyc) finitely generated over ℤ_p, then X(E/F_∞) ∈ 𝔐_H(G). Example: the three conductor-11 curves E₀, E₁, E₂ at p = 5 with L = ℚ(μ₅) (G_L pro-5 and X(E₁/L^cyc) = 0) satisfy Conjecture 5.1.
hypotheses: the proofs use Coates–Howson-type results ([8], [9], [11] of CFKSV: the finiteness of H¹(H_F, E_{p^∞}), Proposition 2.13 and Lemma 2.5 of [9]), Venjakob's pseudo-null theory [26], Schneps' thesis [28] and the two-variable CM main conjecture [27] ; their supplier and primary-proof obligations are recorded as an arithmetic gap
the vanishing X(E₁/ℚ(μ₅)^cyc) = 0 is quoted from [16] (a gap)
proofSteps: Lemma 5.3: the restriction map r_F : X(E/F_∞)_{H_F} → X(E/F^cyc) has finite cokernel (dual to ker t_F ⊂ H¹(H_F, E_{p^∞}), finite), so Y(E/F^cyc) is finitely generated over ℤ_p and X(E/F^cyc) is Λ(Γ_F)-torsion; the rest from [9].
Lemma 5.4: H₀(H_L, Y(E/F_∞)) is Λ(Γ_L)-torsion, and formula (25) of [9] forces its μ-invariant to vanish; Nakayama over the pro-p H_L.
Corollary 5.5 from Lemmas 5.3–5.4 with Schneps and Venjakob; Proposition 5.6 by Nakayama from r_L and an isogeny f : E′ → E whose induced map X(E/F_∞) → X(E′/F_∞) has kernel killed by a power of p.
acceptance: Check that Proposition 5.6's example uses the same F_∞ for all three isogenous curves.

nodes.title: Admissible p-adic Lie extensions and the hypothesis μ = 0
nodes.statement: Let F be a totally real number field and p odd. An admissible p-adic Lie extension F_∞/F is a Galois extension, unramified outside a finite set of primes, with F_∞ totally real, G = Gal(F_∞/F) a p-adic Lie group and F_cyc ⊆ F_∞; put H = Gal(F_∞/F_cyc), Γ = G/H, and fix a finite set Σ of finite primes containing those ramified in F_∞. F_∞/F satisfies μ = 0 if some open pro-p subgroup H′ ≤ H has Gal(M/F_∞^{H′}) finitely generated over ℤ_p, M the maximal abelian pro-p extension of F_∞^{H′} unramified outside Σ; equivalently, the Iwasawa μ-invariant of L(μ_p) vanishes for L with L_cyc = F_∞^{H′}. Equivalently (Lemma 9), X = Gal(M_∞/F_∞) is finitely generated over Λ(H), M_∞ the maximal abelian pro-p extension of F_∞ unramified outside Σ.
hypotheses: F totally real, p odd, Σ finite containing the ramified primes.
proofSteps: Lemma 9: for H′ pro-p, Λ(H′) is local, so by Nakayama X is finitely generated over Λ(H) iff X_{H′} is finitely generated over ℤ_p; the inflation–restriction sequence for Gal(F_Σ/F_∞) ⊆ Gal(F_Σ/F_∞^{H′}) with ℚ_p/ℤ_p coefficients (ArithmeticGaloisDuality R02.2) and the cofiniteness of H^i(H′, ℚ_p/ℤ_p) compare X_{H′} with Gal(M/F_∞^{H′}).
acceptance: μ = 0 is a hypothesis, recorded separately; Ferrero–Washington proves it for abelian L/ℚ, and nothing more general is claimed.

nodes.title: The complex C(F_∞/F)
nodes.statement: For an admissible F_∞/F, C(F_∞/F) = RHom(RΓ_ét(Spec 𝒪_{F_∞}[1/Σ], ℚ_p/ℤ_p), ℚ_p/ℤ_p) ≅ RHom(RΓ(Gal(F_Σ/F_∞), ℚ_p/ℤ_p), ℚ_p/ℤ_p), with H^{−1} = Gal(M_∞/F_∞), H⁰ = ℤ_p and H^i = 0 otherwise. It is a perfect complex of Λ(G)-modules, Λ(Gal(K/F)) ⊗^L_{Λ(G)} C(F_∞/F) ≅ C(K/F) for F ⊆ K ⊆ F_∞ with K/F Galois, and, under μ = 0, it is S-torsion, so it has a class [C(F_∞/F)] ∈ K₀(Λ(G), Λ(G)_S).
hypotheses: F_∞/F admissible; μ = 0 for the class in relative K₀.
This is the dual Galois-cochain complex in degrees −1,0, not the ordinary compact-support cone; compare them only through the requested duality/local correction theorem.
proofSteps: The étale–Galois comparison, since ℚ_p/ℤ_p is a colimit of finite p-groups.

Cohomology: H⁰ = ℤ_p is the dual of H⁰(Gal(F_Σ/F_∞), ℚ_p/ℤ_p); H^{−1} is the dual of Hom(Gal(F_Σ/F_∞), ℚ_p/ℤ_p) = Gal(M_∞/F_∞)^∨; H²(Gal(F_Σ/F_∞), ℚ_p/ℤ_p) = 0 for totally real F_∞ and odd p (weak Leopoldt along F_cyc and ArithmeticGaloisDuality R02.4's cohomological dimension).
Perfectness and base change (1) are Fukaya–Kato's (see the gap on Fukaya–Kato).

S-torsion: its cohomology is finitely generated over Λ(H) by admissible-extension's Lemma 9, so Λ(G)_S ⊗^L C is acyclic (NE.1/s-torsion-iff-finitely-generated); the class is in NE.1/torsion-perfect-complexes.
acceptance: When G has elements of order p, X itself need not have finite projective dimension; the complex, not the module, is what has a class.

nodes.title: Equivariant compactly supported Iwasawa complexes
nodes.statement: Let p be odd, F∞/F a Galois compact p-adic Lie extension containing the cyclotomic tower unramified outside a finite Σ containing p, ramified and archimedean places, and T a finite free Z_p Galois lattice unramified outside Σ. Define RΓ_Iw,c(F∞,T)=Rlim_L RΓ_c(O_(L,Σ),T), with corestriction transitions and left Λ(G)-action. At finite L, compact support is Cone(RΓ(O_(L,Σ),T)→⊕_(v∈Σ_L)RΓ(L_v,T))[−1], with the ordinary odd-primary real-place convention. Greenberg/Selmer local conditions replace the indicated local targets by their specified quotients or mapping fibres. The construction imports continuous Galois cochains, local conditions and the derived inverse limit; it adds the noncommutative coefficient action and comparison squares.
hypotheses: p odd; G=Gal(F∞/F) compact p-adic analytic; F∞ contains the cyclotomic tower; finite ramification set Σ as stated.
T finite free, with continuous Galois action; local conditions and their transition maps are specified.
proofSteps: Use SelmerIwasawaCohomology L2’s mapping-fibre construction and L3’s Iwasawa cochains at the finite layers.
Use compatible corestriction and conjugation maps to give the derived inverse limit its Λ(G)-action.
Compare the global and every local cochain by the same Shapiro bimodule, so base change respects the defining triangle; do not infer the local comparison from the global one alone.
acceptance: For a cyclotomic abelian tower and the same T and local conditions, recover SelmerIwasawaCohomology L3’s complex with identical cohomological degrees.
At a finite real place and odd p, higher C₂-cohomology is zero by averaging; degree-zero invariants still occur in the compact-support triangle.
For Σ enlarged by a finite prime, the difference is the corresponding local correction complex; dropping it changes the determinant.
Taking N=1 gives the identity base-change map on both global and local terms.

sources.match: Uses compactly supported and Selmer determinant complexes with specified local conditions.
The totally real dual complex is the specialized arithmetic input; its comparison with compact support must include duality and shifts.

nodes.title: Perfection, torsion and derived arithmetic base change
nodes.statement: Let p be odd and G have no element of order p. If the equivariant compact-support complex is bounded and all its cohomology groups are finitely generated over Λ(G), then it is perfect, by the finite-global-dimension theorem. Under the global/local Shapiro and duality hypotheses, quotient derived base change and open-subgroup restriction identify it with the corresponding arithmetic complexes and commute with the local triangles. It belongs to Σ_S exactly when its localized cohomology vanishes. In the totally real odd-primary μ=0 setting, the dual complex C has H^(−1)=X_Σ, H⁰=Z_p and Λ(H)-finite cohomology, hence is S-torsion. When G has p-torsion, perfection of that specific C is a separate Fukaya–Kato theorem requested in the source gap; finite global dimension supplies no argument.
hypotheses: For the finite-global-dimension route: p odd, G compact p-adic analytic with no element of order p, bounded complex and finitely generated Λ(G)-cohomology; boundedness and finite generation must come from the stated arithmetic hypotheses, not from rational dimensions alone.

For the comparisons: F∞/F unramified outside finite Σ containing p and infinity, finite-free continuous coefficient lattice and compatible perfect local conditions, with global and local Shapiro/duality supplied.
For the final torsion clause: totally real admissible F∞/F and Kakde μ=0. For a group with p-torsion the specific cochain-perfection theorem is an additional input.
proofSteps: Use the cochain supplier for boundedness and finite generation. Without p-torsion replace the bounded finite-cohomology complex by a finite-projective resolution using global dimension d+1. Import the distinct arithmetic perfection theorem for C if p-torsion is allowed.
Use exact derived base change on the bounded projective model; keep finite correction modules under control in the resulting cohomology long exact sequences.
Apply flatness of canonical Ore localization to test acyclicity on cohomology. For C use the explicit weak-Leopoldt input and the Λ(H)-finiteness criterion of Kakde Lemma 9.
At p=2 this target does not assert perfection of ordinary compact support; the separate real-place correction contract is an open gap.
acceptance: A complex with a single Λ-free cohomology module is perfect but is not S-torsion.
For the totally real cyclotomic specialization H=1, verify H^(−1)=X_Σ and H⁰=Z_p, rather than shifting both degrees by one.
Derived specialization of a two-term resolution [Λ --T→ Λ] at T=0 has two nonzero terms; underived tensor of its cokernel loses Tor₁.

sources.match: States the dual complex’s perfectness and quotient base change and gives the μ=0 finiteness input.

nodes.title: Real-place correction at the prime two
nodes.statement: At p=2 an ordinary real-place local cochain term cannot be erased or replaced by the odd-primary averaging argument. The required extension is a compact-support/local-condition triangle with complete Tate cochains for Gal(C/R)=C₂ at real places and a specified comparison with the chosen arithmetic dual complex. Its bounded/perfect replacement, duality shift and localization class require a separate theorem under explicit hypotheses. This node records that comparison target, not a theorem that the odd-primary complexes already satisfy it.
hypotheses: p=2; number field with real places; a chosen integral Tate-cochain model and arithmetic local conditions.
proofSteps: Compute the real local cohomology and Tate complex explicitly; nonvanishing 2-primary terms rule out the odd-prime simplification.
Request the bounded perfect replacement and its comparison from arithmetic duality and IntegralIwasawaTheory’s all-prime compact-support owner.
Transport a relative class only after that theorem proves both perfection and localized acyclicity.
acceptance: For the trivial Z₂-module, H²(C₂,Z₂)=Z/2, whereas positive cohomology vanishes with Z_p coefficients at odd p.
For a totally imaginary field there is no real-place correction sum.
An alleged p=2 comparison that discards the real Tate term cannot preserve the compact-support triangle.

nodes.title: The conjectural GL₂ p-adic L-function ℒ_E (Conjecture 5.7)
nodes.statement: For an Artin representation ρ of G realised over K_ρ, L(E, ρ, s) = Π_q P_q(E, ρ, q^{−s})^{−1} with P_q(E, ρ, T) = det(1 − Frob_q^{−1}T | (H¹_l(E) ⊗ V_{ρ,λ})^{I_q}); Ω_±(E) are the periods of the Néron differential over the ±-eigenvectors of complex conjugation on H₁(E(ℂ), ℤ); d^±(ρ) are the ±-dimensions of ρ; L_R(E, ρ, s) omits the Euler factors at R = {p} ∪ {q : ord_q(j_E) < 0}; p^{f_ρ} is the p-part of the conductor of ρ; 1 − a_pX + pX² = (1 − uX)(1 − wX) with u ∈ ℤ_p^×; e_p(ρ) is the local ε-factor at p. Assume (103): L(E, ρ, 1)/(Ω_+^{d⁺(ρ)}Ω_−^{d⁻(ρ)}) ∈ ℚ̄ and the analytic continuation of L(E, ρ, s) to s = 1. Let K(F_∞) be the maximal abelian extension of ℚ in F_∞ unramified at p (a finite extension), A the integers of the completion of K(F_∞) at a prime above p, Λ_A(G) = Λ(G) ⊗_{ℤ_p} A and S(A)* the corresponding Ore set, with Λ_A(G)_{S(A)*} = Λ(G)_{S*} ⊗ A. Conjecture 5.7 (p ≥ 5, good ordinary reduction) is the proposition that there is ℒ_E ∈ K₁(Λ_A(G)_{S(A)*}) with ℒ_E(ρ) ≠ ∞ and ℒ_E(ρ) = L_R(E, ρ, 1)/(Ω_+^{d⁺(ρ)}Ω_−^{d⁻(ρ)}) · e_p(ρ) · P_p(ρ̂, u^{−1})/P_p(ρ, w^{−1}) · u^{−f_ρ} for all Artin ρ (107).
hypotheses: a conjecture; the period conjecture (103) and analytic continuation are assumptions of its formulation
the enlarged coefficient ring A comes from the Tamagawa number conjecture (Fukaya–Kato [17], Theorem 4.2.26); evaluation extends to K₁(Λ_A(G)_{S(A)*}) as in §3
proofSteps: Definitions; S(A) is a left and right Ore set by the arguments of §2 (NE.1/canonical-ore-theorem), and Λ_A(G) = Λ(G) ⊗ A since A is free of finite rank over ℤ_p.
acceptance: The abelian specialisation (ρ a Dirichlet character of Γ-type) must recover the Mazur–Swinnerton-Dyer p-adic L-function with the same normalisation, not merely one with the same ideal (the stage's acceptance).

nodes.title: The GL₂ main conjecture (Conjecture 5.8)
nodes.statement: Assume p ≥ 5, good ordinary reduction and X(E/F_∞) ∈ 𝔐_H(G), and let ξ_E be a characteristic element of X(E/F_∞) (NE.2/characteristic-element). nodes.statement: Assume CFKSV Conjecture 5.8, including the 𝔐_H(G) and interpolation hypotheses. When finite it equals |ℒ_E(ρ)|_p^(−[L:Q_p]), with ℒ_E(ρ) the complete period- and Euler-factor-normalized expression (107). The coefficient-field degree and every local factor are retained; no scalar equality with an unnormalized complex L-value is asserted.

nodes.title: The main conjecture for X₁(11) at p = 5: the data and the consistency check
nodes.statement: For E = X₁(11) and p = 5 (continuing NE.3/gl2-euler-example): K(F_∞) = ℚ(μ₁₁)⁺, 5 is inert in it, and A is the integers of the unramified extension of ℚ₅ of degree 5. For the two degree-4 Artin representations ρ₁, ρ₂: d⁺ = d⁻ = 2; f_{ρ₁} = 3, f_{ρ₂} = 5; P₅(ρ₁, X) = 1 − X, P₅(ρ₂, X) = 1; P₅(E, ρ₁, X) = 1 − X + 5X², P₅(E, ρ₂, X) = 1; P₁₁(E, ρ_i, X) = 1; |e₅(ρ₁)|₅ = 5^{−3/2}, |e₅(ρ₂)|₅ = 5^{−5/2}; 1 − a₅X + 5X² = 1 − X + 5X²; and L(E, ρ₁, 1)/(Ω₊Ω₋)² = −2²/(11²√5), L(E, ρ₂, 1)/(Ω₊Ω₋)² = −2⁶/(11²·5√5). Both L-values are nonzero, so with Proposition 3.11 Corollary 5.9 holds for ρ₁, ρ₂; the right-hand side of (107) has the 5-adic valuations predicted by (74), so Corollary 5.10 holds for them too.
hypotheses: the numerical data are quoted from Dokchitser–Dokchitser [15], not recomputed (a gap for formalisation)
this checks consistency, not the conjecture
proofSteps: Insert (108)–(115) into (107): u, w are the roots of Y² − Y + 5 with u ≡ 1, w ≡ 0 mod 5, so v₅(1 − u^{−1}) = v₅(w) = 1 and v₅(1 − w^{−1}) = −1.
ρ₁: v₅ = −1/2 (L-value) + 3/2 (e₅) + (1 − (−1)) (the P₅ ratio) = 3; ρ₂: v₅ = −3/2 + 5/2 + 0 = 1. These match Proposition 3.11's Euler characteristics 5³ and 5 (with m_ρ = 1, ρ_i realised over ℤ₅).
acceptance: The numerical consistency checks give −1/2+3/2+2=3 and −3/2+5/2=1; they do not validate the source L-values independently.

nodes.title: The main conjecture for totally real fields
nodes.statement: For an admissible F_∞/F satisfying μ = 0, MC(F_∞/F) is the proposition: there is a unique ζ(F_∞/F) ∈ K′₁(Λ(G)_S) with ∂(ζ(F_∞/F)) = −[C(F_∞/F)] and ζ(F_∞/F)(ρκ_F^r) = L_Σ(ρ, 1 − r) for every Artin character ρ of G and every positive integer r divisible by [F_∞(μ_p) : F_∞], where κ_F is the p-adic cyclotomic character and L_Σ(ρ, 1 − r) the Klingen–Siegel value with the Euler factors at Σ removed.
hypotheses: μ = 0; p odd; F totally real. Kakde states it as Theorem 11 because he proves it (NE.6).
proofSteps: Definition; the evaluation is NE.3/artin-evaluation on K′₁ (k1-prime), ∂ is the boundary of the localisation sequence, surjective by boundary-surjective-p-torsion.
acceptance: Uniqueness is in K′₁; in K₁ it can fail (Kakde, Remark 12). The formulation in K₁ is equivalent because SK₁(Λ(G)_S) = ker ∂ ∩ ⋂_ρ ker(evaluation at ρ) (Burns, recorded, not planned).
Independence of Σ (Remark 14) is recorded as the test below, not proved here.

nodes.title: Localized zeta interpolation contract
nodes.statement: For a specified perfect S-torsion arithmetic complex C, a specified sign ε∈{1,−1}, an allowed Artin/Tate-twist set A and normalized values I(ρ,r), define ZetaContract(C,ε,A,I) to be the set of ζ∈K₁(Λ_S) with ∂ζ=ε[C] and ev_(ρκ^r)(ζ)=I(ρ,r) wherever ordinary evaluation is defined. At exceptional zeros replace the last equality by the stated leading-term formula, with its Bockstein trivialization. Existence means this set is nonempty; uniqueness means it has at most one element in the specified group, or only after passing to an explicitly named quotient. Periods, removed Euler factors and contragredients are part of I, not adjustable units.
hypotheses: C perfect and S-acyclic; its boundary sign is specified; evaluation maps are defined on the chosen domain.
Interpolation data include coefficient field, periods, Frobenius convention, Artin dual and Euler factors.
proofSteps: Use the existing CFKSV and totally real formulations as two choices of the data, keeping their different signs.
Express the contract as a predicate on actual localized K₁, with a separate quotient version for K′₁.
For leading-term clauses require the semisimplicity/Bockstein data of NE.7; never manufacture these from nonzero interpolation values.
acceptance: For C=[Λ --T→ Λ], the positive-boundary characteristic lift is T, while the Burns–Venjakob characteristic map is T⁻¹ with negative boundary.
Multiplying by a nontrivial integral unit preserves a boundary class but can change the normalized interpolation value; boundary equality does not imply the contract.
If x≠1 belongs to the common kernel of boundary and every evaluation, then ζ and ζx meet the same contract; uniqueness needs an extra kernel theorem.
Changing an Artin representation to its dual without changing the period/local-factor formula is a different contract.
