nodes.title: Ritter–Weiss main theorem with μ = 0
nodes.statement: Let p be odd and K/k a totally real Galois extension with k/Q finite, K containing k_cyc and [K:k_cyc]<∞. Let S contain all archimedean and ramified places and suppose μ_(K/k)=0. There exists Θ∈K₁(QG) with Det Θ=L_(K/k,S) and ∂Θ=℧_(K/k,S). The theorem proves existence; uniqueness in K₁(QG) is not part of its conclusion. Its comparison with the canonical-localization version requires both the localization maps and the refined-module/dual-complex sign comparison. Equivalently, in the source’s μ=0 criterion, L_(K/k,S) lies in Det K₁(B_G), where B_G=Λ∧G is the completed central-regular localization. This completed preimage, rather than the class ℧, is the input of completed-zeta-canonical-descent.
hypotheses: Exactly the odd-prime, finite-over-cyclotomic, totally real and μ=0 hypotheses in the statement.
proofSteps: Apply the logarithmic integrality criterion and the p-elementary reduction.
Use the Möbius congruences and Theorem 7 to lift integral logarithmic pseudomeasures through a central subgroup of exponent p.
Induct on the order of the commutator subgroup and the index of the center. Lemma h detects additive classes by all abelianized restrictions.

Choose a lift with support of minimal size. For its minimal U, restriction to all maximal proper V forces the coefficients to vanish unless U/A is cyclic and the supported coset generates U/A. Lemma g expresses the remaining trace coefficients in a basis; Claim 3 lifts them to τ_G(y(c−1)). This correction preserves deflation modulo C and restriction to A, removes U, and only affects groups containing a conjugate of U, which were already in the support by Claim 1. This contradicts minimal support. Lemmas i–k extend integrality, the relative logarithm and torsion correction componentwise to the prime-to-p factor. The earlier-paper trace/logarithm inputs are listed separately; Proposition 6 now has its explicit analytic proof above.
acceptance: The abelian case reduces to the normalized abelian pseudomeasure theorem with the same S.
No p=2 or arbitrary higher-dimensional statement follows from this theorem.

The completed preimage b has θ̂_P(b)=ζ_P: Det commutes with abelianized restriction, and Det is injective for the commutative semilocal B(U_P^ab). This identifies its normalized components without using a comparison of ℧ with the arithmetic complex.

nodes.title: Conditional Ritter–Weiss SK₁ reduction
nodes.statement: For odd p, the universal vanishing SK₁(QG)=0 for the one-dimensional totally real Galois groups in Ritter–Weiss would follow if SK₁(D_(r,s,F))=0 for every finite unramified F/Q_p and positive r,s. Here O_m is the integer ring of F(ζ_(p^m)), A=O_r[[T]], B=O_(r+s)[[T]], and D_(r,s,F)=(Frac(B)/Frac(A),g,1+T), with g(ζ_(p^(r+s)))=ζ_(p^(r+s))^{1+p^r}. Thus an element u satisfies ub=g(b)u and u^{p^s}=1+T. The source’s Theorem 1A is this reduction; it is not a proof of all the required SK₁ vanishings. No unconditional uniqueness upgrade is exported.
hypotheses: p odd; F/Q_p finite unramified; r,s≥1; compatible p-power roots of unity.
The vanishing for every displayed cyclic division algebra is a premise, presently a recorded gap.
proofSteps: Use the cited Wedderburn-component classification to reduce to a matrix algebra over one of the listed cyclic division algebras.
Use Morita invariance of K₁ and SK₁ and product compatibility.
Normalize a unit exponent m prime to p by the automorphism T↦(1+T)^m−1. Do not replace the unresolved norm-one commutator problem by an asserted surjectivity claim.
acceptance: The hypothesis is a family of SK₁ vanishing assertions, not merely a single split-matrix calculation.
The parameter change with m=1 is the identity; a prime-to-p m has the inverse exponent 1/m in Z_p.
The statement supplies no result at p=2.

nodes.title: Unconditional abelian minus main theorem
nodes.statement: Let H/F be finite abelian CM with F totally real, p odd, H∞/H cyclotomic and G=Gal(H∞/F). Let S,T be disjoint finite sets with S∞∪S_p⊆S, S_ram⊆S∪T and Hyp_p^T: T is not contained in S_ram and H has no nontrivial p-power root of unity congruent to 1 above every place of T∖S_ram. Then over R=Z_p[[G]]^− the source’s covariantly dualized smoothed Selmer module M=Sel_S^T(H∞)_p^− has Fitt_R(M)=(Θ_S^T), and admits an injective square finite-free presentation (hence projective dimension at most one). No μ=0 premise is used. Its comparison with the abstract Picard module’s Pontryagin dual is unconditional; identifying that dual with the Z_p-dual of the Tate module uses μ=0.
hypotheses: Exactly the field, parity and S,T conditions in the statement; complex conjugation defines the minus idempotent (1−j)/2.
The source uses the covariant action (g f)(x)=f(gx) on duals, not an unrecorded contragredient convention.
proofSteps: Import the finite-level smoothed Selmer presentations and their compatible restriction maps from the IntegralIwasawaTheory I.6 extension request.
Apply Theorem 6.28 at every finite layer; Proposition 3.16 and Lemma 4.7 pass the Fitting ideals and the specified Θ elements to the inverse limit.
Use Proposition 4.6’s nonzero-divisor Θ and Proposition 4.9 over the semilocal Iwasawa ring to obtain an injective square presentation.
Use Proposition 7.10’s diagram to identify the Pontryagin dual; invoke μ=0 only for the further Tate-module comparison. These subsidiary proofs and suppliers are recorded precisely as refinements.
acceptance: The idempotent (1−j)/2 requires odd p; it is not an integral two-primary construction.
A finite-level theorem allowing fewer p-adic places in S does not remove S_p⊆S from the Iwasawa theorem.
The theorem cannot remove μ=0 from the nonabelian Kakde or Ritter–Weiss statements.

nodes.title: Bockstein homomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let θ ∈ H^1(G, ℤ_p) = Hom_cont(G, ℤ_p) be G ↠ Γ → ℤ_p with γ ↦ 1; it corresponds to the extension 0 → ℤ_p → E_θ → ℤ_p → 0 with E_θ = ℤ_p² and G acting by (1 θ; 0 1), which gives θ : A· → A·[1] in D^b(Λ(G)). The Bockstein morphism in degree i is B_i = H^{−i}(θ_*) : Tor_i^{Λ(G)}(T_ρ, A·) → Tor_{i−1}^{Λ(G)}(T_ρ, A·), with T_ρ = 𝒪^n a right module through ρ^t. For G = Γ, the triangle A· --T--> A· → ℤ_p ⊗^L A· gives 0 → H^i(A·)_Γ … exact sequences (3), and B_i is the composite H_i(Γ, A·) → H^{−i+1}(A·)^Γ --κ--> H^{−i+1}(A·)_Γ → H_{i−1}(Γ, A·), with κ induced by the identity (Lemma 3.1); so (H_·(Γ, A·), B_·) is a complex (4).
hypotheses: G is a compact p-adic Lie group with a closed normal H and Γ = G/H ≅ ℤ_p, with a fixed generator γ and T = γ − 1; ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) is continuous, 𝒪 = 𝒪_L for L/ℚ_p finite.
proofSteps: E_θ ∈ Ext^1_{Λ(G)}(ℤ_p, ℤ_p) ≅ H^1(G, ℤ_p) (NSW 5.2.14); tensoring A· with it gives the triangle defining θ.

Lemma 3.1: with cone(A·) = cone(T) and the quasi-isomorphism π : cone(A·) → A·_0, θ is (a, b) ↦ (b, 0) (Schneider); for a cycle ā lift to (a, b) with b = −T^{−1}d(a), and the class maps to −T^{−1}d(a), which is the stated composite.
acceptance: The mapping-cone sign convention is BV's: d_cone = (d_B f; 0 −d_A).

nodes.title: Semisimple complexes and the order r(ρ)
nodes.statement: A· ∈ C^p(Λ(Γ)) is semisimple if the Bockstein complex (H_·(Γ, A·), B_·) has ℤ_p-torsion (hence finite) cohomology; Σ^{ss} is the full subcategory of such complexes, and r_Γ(A·) = Σ_i (−1)^{i+1} dim_{ℚ_p}(H^i(A·)^Γ ⊗ ℚ_p) (Definition 3.2). Semisimple complexes have Λ(Γ)-torsion cohomology, and A· ∈ Σ^{ss} iff κ_i ⊗ ℚ_p is bijective in every degree, in which case r_Γ(A·) = Σ(−1)^{i+1} dim H^i(A·)_Γ ⊗ ℚ_p (Remark 3.3). For general G: A· is semisimple at ρ if (H_·(G, A·(ρ^*)), B_·) has ℤ_p-torsion cohomology (Definition 3.11), finite at ρ if H_·(G, A·(ρ^*)) is ℤ_p-torsion (Definition 3.12, so Σ^{fin−ρ} ⊆ Σ^{ss−ρ}), and r_G(A·)(ρ) = Σ(−1)^{i+1} dim_L(H^i(H, A·(ρ^*))^Γ ⊗ L). A· is semisimple at ρ iff A·_ρ = (Λ_𝒪(Γ) ⊗ 𝒪^n) ⊗^L A· is semisimple, with the same Bockstein maps and r_G(A·)(ρ) = r_Γ(A·_ρ) (Lemma 3.13). Over a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer T, a semisimple complex is a finite direct sum of [R --1--> R] and [R --T--> R] (Lemma 3.9).
hypotheses: G is a compact p-adic Lie group with a closed normal H and Γ = G/H ≅ ℤ_p, with a fixed generator γ and T = γ − 1; ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) is continuous, 𝒪 = 𝒪_L for L/ℚ_p finite.
proofSteps: Remark 3.3(ii): Lemma 3.1 gives 0 → cok(κ_{−i}) → ker B_i/im B_{i+1} → ker(κ_{−i+1}) → 0.
Lemma 3.9: T kills H^·(A·); split off [R^d --H--> R^d] with H diagonal in {1, T} from the top degree and induct on length.
Lemma 3.13: 𝒪^n ⊗^L_{Λ(G)} A· ≅ 𝒪 ⊗^L_{Λ_𝒪(Γ)} A·_ρ, and Λ_𝒪(Γ) ⊗^L_{Λ(G)} A· ≅ 𝒪 ⊗^L_{Λ(H)} A·; the Bockstein map is functorial.
acceptance: Σ^{ss} and Σ^{ss−ρ} satisfy (i)–(iii) and (iv′) but not (iv): they are not closed under extensions (finding E11).

nodes.statement: For A· ∈ Σ^{ss}, t(A·) : d_{ℤ_p}(ℤ_p ⊗^L_{Λ(Γ)} A·)_{ℚ_p} ≅ d((H_·(Γ, A·), 0))_{ℚ_p} = d((H_·(Γ, A·), B_·))_{ℚ_p} ≅ 1_{ℚ_p}, using property h) and then e) for the acyclic rational Bockstein complex (Definition 3.4, (5)). nodes.title: The leading term at a representation
nodes.statement: For A· ∈ Σ^{ss−ρ} and a : 1_{Λ(G)} → d_{Λ(G)}(A·), the leading term (A·, a)^*(ρ) ∈ L^× is (−1)^{r_G(A·)(ρ)} times the element of L^× ≅ K_1(L) ≅ Aut(1_L) given by 1_L --L^n ⊗ a--> d_L(L^n ⊗^L_{Λ(G)} A·) --t(A·(ρ^*))--> 1_L (Definition 3.14; for G = Γ and ρ = ρ_triv, Definition 3.7). It gives a homomorphism (−)^*(ρ) : K_1(Λ(G), Σ) → L^× on subcategories Σ ⊆ Σ^{ss−ρ} with (i)–(iii), (iv′). If A· ∈ Σ^{fin−ρ}, the leading term is the value [A·, a](ρ) in the sense of Fukaya–Kato 4.1.5 (Remark 3.15).
hypotheses: G is a compact p-adic Lie group with a closed normal H and Γ = G/H ≅ ℤ_p, with a fixed generator γ and T = γ − 1; ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) is continuous, 𝒪 = 𝒪_L for L/ℚ_p finite.
proofSteps: Well defined on K_1(Λ(G), Σ): relations (1) and (2) are respected by Lemma 3.13(iii) and Lemma 3.6, relation (0) trivially.
Compatibility of Definitions 3.7 and 3.14 for G = Γ, ρ = ρ_triv is immediate.
acceptance: The acceptance case: A· = [R --T--> R] with a_ε from ε ∈ R^× has leading term ε(0) and order r = −1; its shift [R --T--> R][1] has order +1 and leading term ε(0)^{−1} (a vanishing case with its Bockstein determinant); [R --f→R] in degrees −1,0, f(0)≠0, has value f(0)⁻¹ with the identity determinant trivialization.
BV define (−)^*(ρ) on K_1(Λ(G), Σ_{A·}) and claim Σ_{A·} ⊆ Σ^{ss−ρ}; that inclusion fails for the extension-closed Σ_{A·} (E11), so the domain is taken with (iv′).

sources.locator: §3.3, Definition 3.14 and Remark 3.15, pp. 14–15; Definition 3.7, p. 10 (arXiv v2)
sources.match: Definitions 3.7 and 3.14 and Remark 3.15.

nodes.title: Leading terms as leading coefficients of characteristic series
nodes.statement: Let L = [A·, a] with A· ∈ Σ^{ss} for G = Γ, and ch_Γ : K_1(Λ(Γ), Σ^{ss}) → K_1(Q(Γ)) = Q(Γ)^×. Writing F = T^rG(T) with G(0) ∈ L^× (6), (i) r(ch_Γ(L)) = r_Γ(A·), and (ii) (−)^*(ρ_triv) = (−)^*(0) ∘ ch_Γ, where F^*(0) = G(0) (Proposition 3.8). The same holds with 𝒪, L, Λ_𝒪(Γ) and Q_𝒪(Γ) (Remark 3.10).
hypotheses: G is a compact p-adic Lie group with a closed normal H and Γ = G/H ≅ ℤ_p, with a fixed generator γ and T = γ − 1; ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) is continuous, 𝒪 = 𝒪_L for L/ℚ_p finite.
proofSteps: Both maps factor through the localisation R = Λ(Γ)_𝔭 at the augmentation ideal, a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer T and residue field ℚ_p, and K_1(R, Ξ) for the semisimple complexes Ξ over R.
Lemma 3.9 reduces to A· = [R --a--> R] with a = 1 or T; the acyclic case is trivial.

For a = T and the trivialisation a_ε (ε ∈ R^×): ch_Γ(L_ε) = T^{−1}ε, so ch_Γ(L_ε)^*(0) = ε(0). The Bockstein B_1 is ℤ_p --(−1)--> ℤ_p, so the composite in the definition is ℚ_p --ε(0)--> ℚ_p --(B_1)^{−1} = −1--> ℚ_p, of determinant −ε(0); with r_Γ(A·) = −1 = r(ch_Γ(L_ε)) the sign (−1)^{−1} gives L_ε^*(ρ_triv) = ε(0).
acceptance: This is the acceptance example: order −1 with leading term ε(0).

sources.match: Proposition 3.8 with its proof via Lemma 3.9, and Remark 3.10.

nodes.title: Leading terms on the canonical localisation
nodes.statement: For A· ∈ Σ_{S*} ∩ Σ^{ss−ρ} and ch_{G,A·} : K_1(Λ(G), Σ_{A·}) → K_1(Λ(G)_{S*}), let ρ_* : K_1(Λ(G)_{S*}) → K_1(M_n(Q_𝒪(Γ))) ≅ Q_𝒪(Γ)^× be induced by g ↦ ρ(g)ḡ. Then (i) r_G(A·)(ρ) = r_Γ(A·_ρ) = r(ρ_*(ch_{G,A·}(A·))), and (ii) (−)^*(ρ) = (ρ_*(−))^*(0) ∘ ch_{G,A·} (Proposition 3.16). Accordingly F^*(ρ) := ρ_*(F)^*(0) for F ∈ K_1(Λ(G)_{S*}), and F(ρ) := F^*(ρ) when r(ρ_*(F)) = 0.
hypotheses: G is a compact p-adic Lie group with a closed normal H and Γ = G/H ≅ ℤ_p, with a fixed generator γ and T = γ − 1; ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) is continuous, 𝒪 = 𝒪_L for L/ℚ_p finite.
S, S* the canonical Ore sets of CFKSV.
proofSteps: (i) from Lemma 3.13(i), H_i(H, A·(ρ^*)) = H^{−i}(A·_ρ), and Proposition 3.8.
(ii) by composing the square (Λ_𝒪(Γ) ⊗ 𝒪^n) ⊗ − over ch with the square of Proposition 3.8, as in Fukaya–Kato Lemma 4.3.10.
acceptance: F(ρ) agrees with CFKSV's evaluation at ρ (NE.3/artin-evaluation) when r = 0.
The domain K_1(Λ(G), Σ_{A·}) is taken with (iv′), as in leading-term (E11).

sources.match: The canonical Ore sets, ch_{G,A·}, ρ_* and Proposition 3.16 with its proof.

nodes.title: Leading terms as derivatives in the cyclotomic direction
nodes.statement: Fix χ : G ↠ Γ → ℤ_p^× of infinite order, c_{χ,γ} = log_p(χ(γ)) ∈ ℚ_p^×, L = [A·, a] with A· ∈ Σ_{S*}, f_ρ(T) = ρ_*(ch_{G,A·}(L)) ∈ Q_𝒪(Γ)^×, and f_L(ρχ^s) = f_ρ(χ(γ)^s − 1), a p-adic meromorphic function of s ∈ ℤ_p. With r = r_G(A·)(ρ): (i) near 0, L^*(ρχ^s) = L(ρχ^s) = f_L(ρχ^s) for s ≠ 0; (ii) c_{χ,γ}^r L^*(ρ) is the leading coefficient at s = 0 of f_L(ρχ^s); (iii) if r ≥ 0, c_{χ,γ}^r L^*(ρ) = (1/r!)(d^r/ds^r) f_L(ρχ^s)|_{s=0} (Lemma 3.17). For χ = χ_cyc this is partial derivation in the cyclotomic direction (Remark 3.18).
hypotheses: G is a compact p-adic Lie group with a closed normal H and Γ = G/H ≅ ℤ_p, with a fixed generator γ and T = γ − 1; ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) is continuous, 𝒪 = 𝒪_L for L/ℚ_p finite.

The perfect complex A underlying 𝓛 lies in Σ_(ss−ρ), so r=r_G(A)(ρ) is the Laurent order and the Bockstein leading term exists. For a bare scalar f the substitution argument instead uses r=ord_T(f), without asserting an arithmetic determinant comparison.
proofSteps: Near 0, f_{ρχ^s}(0) ∈ L^× for s ≠ 0 and f_{ρχ^s}(T) = f_ρ(χ(γ)^s(T + 1) − 1), so Proposition 3.16 gives (i).
Factor f_ρ = T^rG_ρ with G_ρ(0) = f_ρ^*(0); then f_ρ(χ(γ)^s − 1)/s^r = ((χ(γ)^s − 1)/s)^rG_ρ(χ(γ)^s − 1) → log_p(χ(γ))^rG_ρ(0).
acceptance: For r < 0 only the leading-coefficient statement (ii) holds.

sources.match: Lemma 3.17 with its proof and Remark 3.18.

nodes.title: Generalized Euler–Poincaré characteristics
nodes.statement: For A· ∈ Σ^{ss−ρ}, put H^i_B(G, −) = H^i((H_{−·}(G, −), B_{−·})), χ_add(G, A·(ρ^*)) = Σ_i (−1)^i length_𝒪 H^i_B(G, A·(ρ^*)) and χ_mult = (#κ_L)^{χ_add}. For any trivialisation a and L = [A·, a]: χ_add(G, A·(ρ^*)) = ord_L(L^*(ρ)) and χ_mult(G, A·(ρ^*)) = |L^*(ρ)|_p^{−[L:ℚ_p]} (Proposition 3.19). The Pontryagin dual of the Hochschild–Serre differentials used by Coates–Schneider–Sujatha and others is the Bockstein map, and when A·(ρ^*) ⊗ ℚ_p is acyclic this recovers CFKSV Theorem 3.6, Venjakob Proposition 6.3 and Fukaya–Kato Remark 4.1.13 (Remark 3.20).
hypotheses: G is a compact p-adic Lie group with a closed normal H and Γ = G/H ≅ ℤ_p, with a fixed generator γ and T = γ − 1; ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪) is continuous, 𝒪 = 𝒪_L for L/ℚ_p finite.
proofSteps: Lemma 3.13, property h) and regularity of 𝒪 give 1_𝒪 → d_𝒪(𝒪^n ⊗^L A·) ≅ ∏_i d_𝒪(H^i_B(G, A·(ρ^*)))^{(−1)^i}.
After ⊗L and acyclicity, the leading term is, modulo 𝒪^×, the product of the elements attached to the finite modules H^i_B, whose valuations are their lengths (Remark 2.4).
acceptance: This is the "nonvanishing scalar specialisation" of the acceptance when A· is finite at ρ: the value's valuation is the Euler characteristic.

sources.match: The definitions of χ_add, χ_mult, Proposition 3.19 and Remark 3.20.

nodes.title: The Fukaya–Kato global zeta isomorphism (as a proposition)
nodes.statement: For p odd, U = Spec ℤ[1/S] with S ⊇ {p, ∞}, a motive M over ℚ with a G_ℚ-stable lattice T_p of M_p, F_∞/ℚ a p-adic Lie extension with G = Gal(F_∞/ℚ), and 𝕋 = Λ(G) ⊗ T_p with the diagonal action g(x ⊗ y) = xḡ^{−1} ⊗ gy: the conjecture (Fukaya–Kato 2.3.2) asserts a unique isomorphism ζ_Λ(M) : 1_Λ → d_Λ(RΓ_c(U, 𝕋))^{−1} in 𝒞_Λ whose base change along every motivic ρ : G → GL_n(𝒪_λ) is the composite of ζ_K(M(ρ^*))_{K_λ} : 1 → Δ_K(M(ρ^*))_{K_λ} with the p-adic period-regulator ϑ_λ, where ζ_K(M(ρ^*)) is the isomorphism matching L^*_K(M(ρ^*)) through the period-regulator ϑ_∞ on the fundamental line Δ_K(M) = d(H^0_f(M))^{−1}d(H^1_f(M))d(H^0_f(M^*(1))^*)d(H^1_f(M^*(1))^*)^{−1}d(M_B^+)d(t_M)^{−1} (Conjecture 4.1). It implies the equivariant Tamagawa number conjecture of Burns–Flach. This is a conjectural proposition. The conditional Tate/critical-motive targets explicitly assume its existence and use the typed shift construction below before taking a leading term. Put C=RΓ_c(U,𝕋) and D=C[1]. The determinant shift isomorphism s_C:d(D)≅d(C)⁻¹ defines ζ_D=s_C⁻¹∘ζ:1→d(D). If C is semisimple at ρ, the global leading term means [D,ζ_D]^*(ρ); it is not [C,ζ]. Its order is r(D)=−r(C), its boundary is ∂ch[D,ζ_D]=−[D]=[C], and t(D) is the monoidal inverse of t(C) under s_C. Monoidal inversion sends d(C)→1 to d(C)⁻¹→1; it is distinct from reversing the arrow of a morphism.
hypotheses: p odd; the finiteness of motivic cohomology, ϑ_∞ and ϑ_λ are themselves conjectural inputs (standard conjectures).
proofSteps: Definitions only: RΓ_c(U, 𝕋) is perfect over Λ(G) (Fukaya–Kato; NE.4), and the base change is property i) of the determinant functor.

Use the exact triangle C→0→C[1] and determinant multiplicativity to construct s_C. Shift preserves semisimplicity and negates r. The same triangle and BV Lemma 3.6 identify t(D) with the monoidal inverse of t(C). This gives a typed composite 1→d(C)⁻¹→1 without replacing ζ by its monoidal inverse. The boundary follows from ∂ch[A,a]=−[A].

For a trivialization a:1→d(C), let a^⊗⁻¹:1→d(C)⁻¹ denote its monoidal inverse. This notation differs from the composition inverse a⁻¹:d(C)→1. The pair [C[1],s_C⁻¹a^⊗⁻¹] is the negative of [C,a], and has inverse characteristic function. For a given global ζ:1→d(C)⁻¹ the corresponding a is ζ^⊗⁻¹, so this identity preserves the given ζ rather than silently inverting its arithmetic values.
acceptance: This is a proposition with named conjectural inputs. The Tate-motive and critical-motive targets state the conditional leading-term formulas of Burns–Venjakob §§5–6.

sources.match: §§4.1–4.3: compactly supported cohomology, the fundamental line, the period-regulators, and Conjecture 4.1 (Fukaya–Kato 2.3.2).

nodes.title: Descent for the Tate motive at ρ under Leopoldt (BV Lemma 5.1)
nodes.statement: Fix ρ ∈ R_{ℂ_p}(Ḡ) with Leopoldt's conjecture valid at ρ, i.e. (ℚ_p ⊗ ker λ_p)^ρ = 0 for λ_p : O_E[1/p]^× ⊗ ℤ_p → ∏_{w|p}E_w^× ⊗̂ ℤ_p. (i) (H^i_c(U, 𝕋_E) ⊗ ℚ_p)^ρ is (cok λ_p ⊗ ℚ_p)^ρ for i = 2, (ℚ_p)^ρ for i = 3, and 0 otherwise. (ii) RΓ_c(U, 𝕋) ∈ Σ_{ss−ρ} and r_G(RΓ_c(U, 𝕋))(ρ) = ⟨ρ, 1⟩ = dim_{ℂ_p}(ℚ_p)^ρ. (iii) Under (i), the Bockstein morphism (B²)^ρ : H²_c → H³_c is induced by log_{p,γ,E} : ∏_{w|p}E_w^× ⊗̂ ℤ_p → ℤ_p, (e_w) ↦ −Σ_w c_γ^{−1}log_p(N_{E_w/ℚ_p}(e_w)).
hypotheses: p odd; F_∞/ℚ totally real Galois, containing ℚ_cyc, unramified outside a finite set S ∋ p, with G = Gal(F_∞/ℚ) a compact p-adic Lie group, H = Gal(F_∞/ℚ_cyc), Γ = G/H; E ⊆ F_∞ finite over ℚ with E ∩ ℚ_cyc = ℚ and E_w ∩ ℚ_{p,cyc} = ℚ_p for w | p (condition (15)); Ḡ = Gal(E/ℚ); 𝕋 = Λ(G) with σ acting by multiplication by χ_cyc(σ̄)σ̄^{−1}; U = Spec ℤ[1/S]; c_γ = c_{χ_cyc,γ}.
proofSteps: (i): the triangle RΓ_c(U, 𝕋_E) → RΓ(U, 𝕋_E) → ⊕_{ℓ∈S}RΓ(ℚ_ℓ, 𝕋_E) with H^i(O_E[1/S], ℤ_p(1)) and H^i(E_w, ℤ_p(1)); H²_c ⊗ ℚ_p ≅ cok λ_p ⊗ ℚ_p always, and (H¹_c ⊗ ℚ_p)^ρ = 0 iff (ker λ_p ⊗ ℚ_p)^ρ = 0 since E is totally real.
(ii): (15) gives Gal(E_cyc/ℚ) ≅ Γ × Ḡ; RΓ_c(U, 𝕋)_ρ ≅ O^n ⊗ RΓ_c(U, 𝕋_{E_cyc}) (18), and Lemma 3.13 with the semisimplicity criterion of Remark 3.3(ii).
(iii): compare the global Bockstein with the local ones B¹_w through the triangle, then with B¹_p on RΓ(ℚ_{p,cyc}, ℤ_p(1)), which is c_γ^{−1}·log_p.
acceptance: Check the trivial character ρ = 1 with E = ℚ: ⟨1, 1⟩ = 1, cok λ_p = (ℚ_p^× ⊗̂ ℤ_p)/⟨p⟩ ≅ 1 + pℤ_p, so cok λ_p ⊗ ℚ_p ≅ ℚ_p via log_p, and the Bockstein is −c_γ^{−1}log_p.

sources.match: Leopoldt's conjecture as injectivity of λ_p, and Lemma 5.1.

nodes.title: The p-adic Stark conjecture at s = 1 (Serre; BV Conjecture 5.2)
nodes.statement: For ρ ∈ R_{ℂ_p}(Ḡ), let L_{p,S}(s, ρ) be Greenberg's S-truncated p-adic Artin L-function (L_{p,S}(n, ρ) = L_S(n, ρω^{n−1}) for n < 0) and L^*_{p,S}(1, ρ) := lim_{s→1}(s − 1)^{⟨ρ,1⟩}L_{p,S}(s, ρ). Let μ_∞ : ℂ ⊗ log_∞(O_E^×) ≅ ℂ ⊗ E₀ (E₀ the trace-zero part of E) and μ_p : ℚ_p ⊗ log_∞(O_E^×) → ℚ_p ⊗ E₀ the maps induced by exp_∞ followed by λ_p and log_p (19). Require det μ_p on the ρ-part to be nonzero as part of P-Stark(ρ), equivalently use the corresponding Leopoldt input for that part. The conjecture then asserts that L^*_{p,S}(1, ρ) is the leading term of L_{p,S}(s, ρ) at s = 1 and, for every ℚ[Ḡ]-isomorphism g : E₀ → O_E^× ⊗ ℚ, L^*_{p,S}(1, ρ)/det_{ℂ_p}((ℂ_p ⊗ μ_p) ∘ (ℂ_p ⊗ g))^ρ = L^*_S(1, ρ)/det_ℂ(μ_∞ ∘ (ℂ ⊗ g))^ρ, the two sides compared through a fixed j : ℂ_p ≅ ℂ.
hypotheses: p odd; F_∞/ℚ totally real Galois, containing ℚ_cyc, unramified outside a finite set S ∋ p, with G = Gal(F_∞/ℚ) a compact p-adic Lie group, H = Gal(F_∞/ℚ_cyc), Γ = G/H; E ⊆ F_∞ finite over ℚ with E ∩ ℚ_cyc = ℚ and E_w ∩ ℚ_{p,cyc} = ℚ_p for w | p (condition (15)); Ḡ = Gal(E/ℚ); 𝕋 = Λ(G) with σ acting by multiplication by χ_cyc(σ̄)σ̄^{−1}; U = Spec ℤ[1/S]; c_γ = c_{χ_cyc,γ}.
A fixed isomorphism j : ℂ_p ≅ ℂ.
The quotient formulation includes nonvanishing of its p-adic regulator determinant; without it only a cross-multiplied identity is meaningful and does not itself imply nonvanishing.
proofSteps: Well-definedness: log_∞(O_E^×) is a lattice in ℝ ⊗ E₀ (Dirichlet), so μ_∞ is an isomorphism; (19) factors through ℚ_p ⊗ E₀, so μ_p is an isomorphism under Leopoldt.
Independence of g: changing g multiplies both determinants by the same algebraic number det(ℚ ⊗ h)^ρ.
acceptance: Check that Remark 5.3's point is recorded: Tate's formulation (Chapter VI §5) is imprecise about "log U" and μ_p, and BV's statement is the clarification.

sources.match: Greenberg's L_{p,S}, the maps μ_∞, μ_p and Conjecture 5.2.

nodes.title: The p-adic Stark conjecture for permutation characters (BV Remark 5.4, after Colmez)
nodes.statement: For a subgroup J ⊆ Ḡ and ρ = Ind_J^{Ḡ}1_J, P-Stark(ρ) holds iff the residue at s = 1 of the minimally p-truncated p-adic zeta function of E^J is nonzero and equal to 2^{[E^J:ℚ]−1}hR_p e_p/√|d|, with e_p = ∏_{v|p}(1 − Nv^{−1}); by Colmez this holds iff Leopoldt's conjecture holds for E^J. Leopoldt for E implies it for every E^J. For the general S-truncated function multiply this displayed residue by ∏_(v∈S_f(E^J),v∤p)(1−Nv⁻¹). Keep the same factors on the complex side in the induction comparison.
hypotheses: p odd; F_∞/ℚ totally real Galois, containing ℚ_cyc, unramified outside a finite set S ∋ p, with G = Gal(F_∞/ℚ) a compact p-adic Lie group, H = Gal(F_∞/ℚ_cyc), Γ = G/H; E ⊆ F_∞ finite over ℚ with E ∩ ℚ_cyc = ℚ and E_w ∩ ℚ_{p,cyc} = ℚ_p for w | p (condition (15)); Ḡ = Gal(E/ℚ); 𝕋 = Λ(G) with σ acting by multiplication by χ_cyc(σ̄)σ̄^{−1}; U = Spec ℤ[1/S]; c_γ = c_{χ_cyc,γ}.
proofSteps: Inductivity of L-functions reduces ρ = Ind 1_J to the Dedekind and p-adic zeta functions of E^J; the complex side is the analytic class number formula (AnalyticNumberTheory AN.4).
Colmez 1988 (the p-adic class number formula for totally real fields; cited, requested from AutomorphicPadicLFunctions L3).
acceptance: Check E^J = ℚ: the formula reduces to Res_{s=1}ζ_p(s) = 1 − 1/p (Kubota–Leopoldt).
For E^J=Q and S_f={p,ℓ}, the residue is (1−p⁻¹)(1−ℓ⁻¹), whereas the minimally p-truncated residue has only the first factor.

sources.match: Remark 5.4 (with Tate's remark p. 138 and Colmez).

nodes.title: Tate-motive interpolation with the global determinant shift
nodes.statement: Assume P-Stark(ρ) for all characters of Ḡ and existence of the Fukaya–Kato zeta isomorphism. Put C=RΓ_c(U,𝕋), D=C[1], m=⟨ρ,1⟩ and ζ_D=s_C⁻¹ζ_Λ(𝕋):1→d(D). Then C and D are semisimple at ρ, r_G(C)(ρ)=m, r_G(D)(ρ)=−m, and c_γ^{−m}·[D,ζ_D]^*(ρ)=L^*_(p,S)(1,ρ). The associated meromorphic function in the cyclotomic variable has order −m at zero, and its leading coefficient is c_γ^{−m}[D,ζ_D]^*(ρ). This is the reconstructed formula in the packet’s typed convention, not BV’s printed exponent in (20).
hypotheses: p odd; F_∞/ℚ totally real Galois, containing ℚ_cyc, unramified outside a finite set S ∋ p, with G = Gal(F_∞/ℚ) a compact p-adic Lie group, H = Gal(F_∞/ℚ_cyc), Γ = G/H; E ⊆ F_∞ finite over ℚ with E ∩ ℚ_cyc = ℚ and E_w ∩ ℚ_{p,cyc} = ℚ_p for w | p (condition (15)); Ḡ = Gal(E/ℚ); 𝕋 = Λ(G) with σ acting by multiplication by χ_cyc(σ̄)σ̄^{−1}; U = Spec ℤ[1/S]; c_γ = c_{χ_cyc,γ}.
The Fukaya–Kato isomorphism ζ_{Λ(G)}(𝕋) (Conjecture 4.1) is assumed to exist.
proofSteps: Use the shift/trivialization interface of fukaya-kato-zeta-isomorphism: the given global ζ is transported to D=C[1], never inverted. The localization boundary is +[C]; the original dual Galois complex of NE.4 is a different complex.
P-Stark implies Leopoldt for E by padic-stark-permutation-case. Lemma 5.1 gives semisimplicity, r(C)=m and B²=−c_γ⁻¹·trace∘log_p on the surviving H²_c,H³_c. Hence D has r=−m.

Write Δ=d(H²_c)⁻¹d(H³_c)=d(D) after the cohomology comparison. The canonical trivialization of this inverse line uses the inverse determinant of B². It therefore contributes (−c_γ)^m, rather than (−c_γ⁻¹)^m. The sign (−1)^{r(D)}=(−1)^m cancels that minus sign.

The given global ζ specializes, by Conjecture 4.1 and BV (21)–(23), to L^*_S(1,ρ) times the complex-to-p-adic regulator comparison in Δ. Composing with t(D) gives [D,ζ_D]^*=c_γ^m·L^*_S(1,ρ)·ξ, where ξ=det(μ_p∘g)^ρ/det(μ_∞∘g)^ρ. P-Stark identifies L^*_S·ξ=L^*_(p,S)(1,ρ). Thus the normalized result has c_γ exponent −m.

Apply Lemma 3.17 to the correctly typed pair [D,ζ_D]. Since r(D)=−m, cyclotomic substitution T=χ_cyc(γ)^s−1 multiplies its Laurent leading coefficient by c_γ^{−m}. For m>0 this is a pole/residue calculation, not an ordinary derivative of nonnegative order.
acceptance: For E=Q and ρ=1 choose a basis u of H²_c with log_p u=ℓ and the usual basis of H³_c. Then ζ=L^*_S(1,1)·ℓ in d(H²_c)⁻¹d(H³_c), B²=−ℓ/c_γ, t(D)=−c_γ/ℓ and the leading sign is −1. Their product is c_γ L^*_S(1,1); multiplying by c_γ⁻¹ gives the p-adic residue. An exponent +1 fails this scalar test.
If γ is replaced by γ^a for a∈Z_p^×, then c_(γ^a)=a c_γ and B² scales by a⁻¹. The pole coefficient [D,ζ_D]^* scales by a^m, so c_γ^{−m}[D,ζ_D]^* is invariant.
For m=0 the shift still types the inverse determinant line; no cyclotomic correction factor occurs. The regulator and zeta existence assumptions remain substantive.

sources.match: Theorem 5.5, Remark 5.6 and the proof.
The given determinant map and Bockstein, combined by the explicitly reconstructed shift, force the negative c_γ exponent. The untyped formula (20) is not quoted as the corrected statement.

nodes.title: The interpolation formula for ℚ-rational characters under Leopoldt (BV Corollary 5.7, corrected scope)
nodes.statement: If Leopoldt's conjecture holds for E at p, then for every ℚ-valued character ρ of Ḡ there is n_ρ ≥ 1 with (c_γ^{−⟨ρ,1⟩}·[RΓ_c(U,𝕋)[1],ζ_D]^*(ρ))^{n_ρ} = L^*_{p,S}(1, ρ)^{n_ρ}; for a permutation character one can take n_ρ = 1. (BV state this for "ℚ_p-rational" characters; the proof covers ℚ-valued ones, see NoncommutativeAndEquivariantIwasawa/E12.) Here ζ_D is the unchanged global map transported along d(RΓ_c[1])≅d(RΓ_c)⁻¹, as in tate-motive-interpolation.
hypotheses: p odd; F_∞/ℚ totally real Galois, containing ℚ_cyc, unramified outside a finite set S ∋ p, with G = Gal(F_∞/ℚ) a compact p-adic Lie group, H = Gal(F_∞/ℚ_cyc), Γ = G/H; E ⊆ F_∞ finite over ℚ with E ∩ ℚ_cyc = ℚ and E_w ∩ ℚ_{p,cyc} = ℚ_p for w | p (condition (15)); Ḡ = Gal(E/ℚ); 𝕋 = Λ(G) with σ acting by multiplication by χ_cyc(σ̄)σ̄^{−1}; U = Spec ℤ[1/S]; c_γ = c_{χ_cyc,γ}.
Leopoldt's conjecture for E at p; the Fukaya–Kato isomorphism exists.
proofSteps: Artin's induction theorem: for ℚ-valued ρ, n_ρ·ρ = Σ_H n_H·Ind_H^{Ḡ}1_H with integers n_H (Tate, Chapitre II, Théorème 1.2).
Both sides of (20) are additive and inductive in ρ; padic-stark-permutation-case (via Colmez) gives (20) for each Ind_H 1_H under Leopoldt.

Use the corrected, shifted formula with exponent −⟨ρ,1⟩ for each permutation character. Multiplicativity of the normalized leading terms then gives the n_ρ-th-power identity. Artin induction does not require P-Stark for non-permutation irreducibles individually.
acceptance: Check the scope: the permutation characters Ind_H 1_H are ℚ-valued, so only ℚ-valued n_ρ·ρ are ℤ-combinations of them; a ℚ_p-valued cubic character (p ≡ 1 mod 3) is not.
For the trivial character n_ρ=1 and the residue normalization is c_γ⁻¹[D,ζ_D]^*. This agrees with the rank-one Bockstein test, not the source’s untyped c_γ formula.

nodes.title: The local ε-isomorphism ε_{p,L}(V) and Fukaya–Kato's local conjecture (BV §6.1, Conjecture 6.1)
nodes.statement: Fix t = (t_n) a generator of ℤ_p(1) and ψ_p : ℚ_p → Q̄_p^× with kernel ℤ_p, 1/p^n ↦ t_n. For a de Rham L-representation V of G_{ℚ_p}, with L̃ = Q̂_p^nr ⊗ L, Γ^*(j) = Γ(j) = (j − 1)! for j > 0 and Res_{s=j}Γ(s) = (−1)^j((−j)!)^{−1} for j ≤ 0, h(j) = dim_L gr^jD_dR(V) and Γ_L(V) = ∏_j Γ^*(j)^{−h(−j)}, ε_{p,L}(V) : 1_{L̃} → (d_L(RΓ(ℚ_p, V))d_L(V))_{L̃} is the product of Γ_L(V), η_l(V)·η_l(V^*(1))^* and Fukaya–Kato's ε_dR(V) : 1 → d(V)d(D_dR(V))^{−1} (which involves Deligne's ε(D_pst(V))). Conjecture 6.1 (Fukaya–Kato 3.4.3): for 𝕋 = Λ ⊗ T there is a unique ε_{p,Λ}(𝕋) : 1_{Λ̃} → (d_Λ(RΓ(ℚ_p, 𝕋))d_Λ(𝕋))_{Λ̃} (Λ̃ = W(F̄_p)⟦G⟧) whose base change along each ρ : G → GL_n(O) is ε_{p,L}(T(ρ^*)).
hypotheses: L/ℚ_p finite; V de Rham; the Haar measure and t are fixed and suppressed.
proofSteps: Definitions; ε_dR(V) exists by Fukaya–Kato Proposition 3.3.5 (cited, source not freely available).
acceptance: Check the Γ-factor convention on V = ℚ_p(1): D_dR has one jump at j = −1, so Γ_L(V) = Γ^*(1)^{−1} = 1; on V = ℚ_p it is Γ^*(0)^{−1} = 1.

nodes.title: Dabrowski–Panchishkin representations and their Selmer complexes (BV §6.2, Lemma 6.2)
nodes.statement: A representation W of G_ℚ satisfies (DP) if it is de Rham and has a G_{ℚ_p}-subrepresentation Ŵ with the natural map D_dR(Ŵ)→t_p(W):=D_dR(W)/Fil⁰D_dR(W) is an isomorphism; then 0 → Ŵ → W → W̃ → 0 with D⁰_dR(Ŵ) = t_p(W̃) = 0, and Z = W^*(1) satisfies (DP) with Ẑ = W̃^*(1). The Selmer complexes SC_U(Ŵ, W) and SC(Ŵ, W) are the mapping fibres of RΓ(U, W) → RΓ(ℚ_p, W/Ŵ) ⊕ ⊕_{ℓ∈S_f∖S_p}RΓ(ℚ_ℓ, W) (resp. RΓ_{/f}(ℚ_ℓ, W) with RΓ_{/f} = cone(RΓ_f → RΓ)). Conditions: (A1) P_ℓ(W, 1)P_ℓ(Z, 1) ≠ 0 for ℓ ∈ S_f ∖ S_p; (B1) P_p(W, 1)P_p(Z, 1) ≠ 0; (C1) P_p(W̃, 1)P_p(Z̃, 1) ≠ 0 (each with equivalent forms). Lemma 6.2: under (A1) the complexes at ℓ ≠ p are acyclic; under (C1), RΓ_{/f}(ℚ_p, X) ≅ RΓ(ℚ_p, X̃) and RΓ_f(ℚ_p, X) ≅ RΓ(ℚ_p, X̂); under both, SC_U(Ŵ, W) ≅ RΓ_f(ℚ, W).
hypotheses: W a finite-dimensional L-representation of G_{ℚ,S}; P_ℓ(V, u) = det(1 − φ_ℓu | V^{I_ℓ}) (ℓ ≠ p), det(1 − φ_pu | D_cris(V)) (ℓ = p), φ geometric Frobenius.
proofSteps: (A1): local duality and the Euler characteristic formula make RΓ(ℚ_ℓ, X) acyclic.
(C1): complexes of vector spaces are quasi-isomorphic to their cohomology, and RΓ(ℚ_p, X̂) ≅ RΓ_f(ℚ_p, X̂) ≅ RΓ_f(ℚ_p, X) (Fukaya–Kato 4.1.7); compare the two triangles.
(iii) from (i), (ii) and the definitions.
acceptance: For an abelian variety with good ordinary reduction, use the ordinary representation in BV Example 6.3. For a split Tate elliptic curve and trivial ρ, check that (B1) holds but (C1) fails: do not retain Example 6.3’s contrary B1 assertion (E31).
W=Q_p(1) has Fil⁰D_dR(W)=0 but t_p(W) one-dimensional. The printed condition Fil⁰D_dR(Ŵ)=t_p(W) would incorrectly reject this example (E25).

nodes.title: Nekovář's p-adic height as a Bockstein map; semisimplicity iff non-degenerate (BV §6.2, Propositions 6.4, 6.6)
nodes.statement: Nekovář's height h_p(W) : H¹_f(ℚ, W) × H¹_f(ℚ, Z) → L (his h̃_{π,1,1}, agreeing up to sign with Schneider, Perrin-Riou, Mazur–Tate and Zarhin) has adjoint equal to H¹_f(ℚ, W) ≅ H¹(SC_U) →^B H²(SC_U) ≅ H²_f(ℚ, W) ≅ H¹_f(ℚ, Z)^* with B the Bockstein of SC_U(𝕋̂_{cyc,ρ}, 𝕋_{cyc,ρ}) (32)–(33). Descent (Proposition 6.4, Fukaya–Kato 1.6.5): L_n ⊗_{Λ,ρ} commutes with RΓ(U, ·), RΓ_c(U, ·), RΓ(ℚ_ℓ, ·) and SC_U, and with RΓ_f(ℚ_ℓ, ·) for ℓ ∉ Υ ∪ S_p, while SC descends only up to the triangle (34) over ℓ ∈ Υ. Proposition 6.6: under (A1), (C1) and (D2), SC_U(𝕋̂_{cyc,ρ}, 𝕋_{cyc,ρ}) ∈ Σ_ss iff h_p(W) is non-degenerate (F), and then r_Γ(SC_U)=−h and r_Γ(SC_U[1])=h for h=dim_L H¹_f(ℚ,W). The sign for the unshifted SC_U corrects the rank assertion in the printed Proposition 6.6.
hypotheses: W = N_λ = V ⊗ [ρ]^*_λ for a motive M satisfying (DP) and a critical twist; (D2): H⁰_f(ℚ, W) = H⁰_f(ℚ, Z) = 0; Υ the primes ℓ ≠ p of infinite ramification in F_∞.
proofSteps: (32)–(33): Nekovář, Selmer Complexes, the sentence after (11.1.3.2) and Theorem 11.3.9 (cited, gap).
Proposition 6.6: under (D2), H^i(SC_U(Ŵ, W)) = 0 for i ≠ 1, 2, and semisimplicity is the invertibility of the Bockstein in degree 1, which is (F).

For the rank, localize O[[T]] at (T). A semisimple torsion perfect complex over this DVR is a direct sum, up to acyclic terms, of elementary blocks [R --T→R] in adjacent degrees. Specialization in degrees 1,2 with invertible degree-1 Bockstein leaves h such blocks in degrees 1,2. Each has ordinary cohomology R/T in degree 2, and contributes (−1)³=−1 to the rank definition. Thus r(SC_U)=−h, while its shift contributes +h. Local finite Euler complexes assumed acyclic at ρ contribute rank zero.
acceptance: Check Example 6.5: for an abelian variety over ℚ, (D1) and (D2) hold, but non-degeneracy (F) is open except Bertrand's CM result.

For one block [R --T→R] in degrees 1,2, the only ordinary cohomology is H²=R/T; BV Definition 3.2 gives r=−1. Its derived special fiber has H¹=H²=L. Counting the dimension of H¹ of that fiber as +r of the unshifted complex gives the wrong sign.

nodes.title: Critical-motive interpolation on shifted Selmer complexes
nodes.statement: Assume W satisfies (A1), (B1), (C1), (D1) and (F), and that ζ_Λ(M) (Conjecture 4.1) and ε_{p,Λ}(𝕋̂) (Conjecture 6.1) exist. Then SC_U(𝕋̂, 𝕋) and SC(𝕋̂, 𝕋) belong to Σ_(ss−ρ), h=dim_L H¹_f(ℚ,W), r_G(SC_U)(ρ)=r_G(SC)(ρ)=−h, and r=r_G(SC_U[1])(ρ)=r_G(SC[1])(ρ)=h, and the leading term 𝓛^*(ρ) (resp. 𝓛_U^*(ρ)) of the Fukaya–Kato p-adic L-function equals (−1)^r·L^*_{K,B}(M(ρ^*))/(Ω_∞(M(ρ^*))R_∞(M(ρ^*)))·Ω_p(M(ρ^*))R_p(M(ρ^*))·Γ(V̂)^{−1}·P_{L,p}(Ŵ^*(1), 1)/P_{L,p}(Ŵ, 1) (38), with L^*_{K,B} truncated at B = Υ ∪ S_p (resp. B = S ∖ S_∞), Ω_∞, R_∞ the archimedean period and regulator (42)–(43), Ω_p the p-adic period (46) and R_p = det h_p(W) (50). In this formula 𝓛_U:1→d(SC_U)⁻¹ is the zeta/epsilon composite of the proof, transported to d(SC_U[1]); likewise for 𝓛 and SC[1]. The symbols 𝓛_U^*,𝓛^* mean these shifted pairs, with boundary +[SC_U],+[SC]. The scalar expression (38) is retained, with its r attached to the shifted complexes.
hypotheses: The hypotheses of height-pairing-bockstein and of Fukaya–Kato's Conjectures 4.1 and 6.1.
Include (D2), the motivic-to-Bloch–Kato Selmer comparison, or supply the named regulator/period comparison proving its equivalence to (D1). Nondegeneracy alone is not that comparison.
proofSteps: Type the zeta/epsilon composite on the inverse line: 1 --ζ→d(RΓ_c)⁻¹ --β·ε⁻¹→d(SC_U)⁻¹ ≅d(SC_U[1]). Use this map as a_U in [SC_U[1],a_U]. The analogous Euler-factor adjustment gives a in [SC[1],a]. There is no inversion of ζ or of its normalized arithmetic factors. The characteristic boundaries are +[SC_U] and +[SC]. The positive determinant targets (36)–(37) cannot be used literally for these composites.

Model: Fukaya–Kato Theorem 4.2.26 (as amplified by Venjakob, proof of Theorem 6.4). Choose good bases γ, δ of M_B^+ and t_M and bases P^∨, P of H¹_f(N), H¹_f(N^*(1)); can = can_{γ′,δ′}·can_{P^∨,P} identifies ζ_K(N) with L^*_K(M)/(Ω_∞R_∞)·can.

𝓛_U^*(ρ) is the product of the factors (44)–(50): the complex leading term over Ω_∞R_∞; Γ_L(Ŵ)^{−1}; the p-adic period Ω_p; the Euler factors at ℓ ≠ p; {P_{L,p}(W, u)P_{L,p}(Ŵ, u)^{−1}}_{u=1}; P_{L,p}(Ŵ^*(1), 1); and the p-adic regulator R_p = det h_p(W), which is t(SC_U[1](ρ^*)) under the coherent determinant shift identification: with H¹=V, H²=V′ and B¹=b, the inverse line is d(V)d(V′)⁻¹ and its trivialization has scalar det b. The leading-term definition contributes the separate sign (−1)^h. Thus the inverse line gives R_p, not its reciprocal.
For 𝓛^*(ρ) use the triangle SC_U(Ŵ, W) → L_n ⊗ SC(𝕋̂, 𝕋) → ⊕_{S_f∖(S_p∪Υ)}RΓ_f(ℚ_ℓ, W) and L^*_{K,Υ′} = L^*_{K,B′}∏_{B∖Υ}P_{L,ℓ}(W, 1)^{−1}.
acceptance: Check Remark 6.8: without (B1), replace P_{L,p}(Ŵ, 1) by the leading coefficient of P_{L,p}(Ŵ, p^s) at s = 0 (the exceptional-zero situation).
Check Example 6.9: for an elliptic curve and F_∞ = ℚ(E[p^∞]), (38) predicts the leading terms of the CFKSV p-adic L-function 𝓛_E at Artin characters with non-degenerate heights.

For one Selmer block with special-fiber B¹=b, t(SC_U)=b⁻¹, t(SC_U[1])=b, r(SC_U)=−1 and r(SC_U[1])=1. With global factor A into the inverse line, the shifted leading term is −Ab. Replacing ζ by its inverse would give a different scalar.

nodes.title: Orders admitted for noncommutative Fitting invariants
nodes.statement: A Fitting order is an o-order Λ in a finite-dimensional separable semisimple algebra A over F=Frac(o), where o is an integrally closed commutative noetherian complete local domain. Thus Λ is a finite torsion-free o-subalgebra with FΛ=A. Fix a containing maximal order Λ′ for computations, retaining its center ζ(Λ′), and the componentwise reduced norm on every matrix algebra over A. A one-dimensional Iwasawa algebra with an open central Γ₀≅Z_p is such an order over o=Z_p[[Γ₀]]. This is the admitted order data for NE.7, not a definition of arbitrary noncommutative fraction rings.
hypotheses: o integrally closed, commutative, noetherian, complete and local; Λ finite torsion-free over o; A=F⊗Λ finite-dimensional separable semisimple.
proofSteps: Import the ambient finite-dimensional algebra, orders and reduced norms; package exactly the hypotheses Nickel Definition 2.1 needs.
For the Iwasawa example use the finite central crossed-product presentation and semisimple total quotient.
Separate ζ(Λ), ζ(Λ′) and ζ(A) throughout; reduced norms of integral matrices need not lie in ζ(Λ).
acceptance: For Λ=M₂(Z₃), take o=Z₃ and A=M₂(Q₃); the reduced norm is the 2×2 determinant.
For Λ=Z_p[C_p], A=Q_p[C_p] is semisimple despite p dividing the group order; semisimplicity is required over F, not over the residue field.
For Λ=Z_p[[Z_p]], use o=Λ and A=Frac(Λ); the coefficient domain need not be a DVR.
An arbitrary higher-dimensional nonabelian Iwasawa algebra is not admitted by the central dimension-one construction.

nodes.title: Integrality ring and denominator ideal
nodes.statement: For a Fitting order Λ⊆Λ′⊆A, define I(Λ) as the ζ(Λ)-module generated by nr(H) for square matrices H over Λ of all sizes; it is a commutative order between ζ(Λ) and ζ(Λ′). Let H* be the generalized adjoint computed from the reduced characteristic polynomials of the simple factors, so H*H=HH*=nr(H)I. Define H(Λ)={x∈ζ(Λ): xH* has entries in Λ for every square H over Λ}. It is a central ideal satisfying H(Λ)I(Λ)=H(Λ)⊆ζ(Λ). The central conductor F(Λ)={x∈ζ(Λ′):xΛ′⊆Λ} lies in H(Λ).
hypotheses: The Fitting order hypotheses and its reduced norms; all matrix sizes enter the definitions.
proofSteps: Use reduced Cayley–Hamilton in each simple factor to form the generalized adjoint.
Block sums and matrix products show that the norm-generated module is a ring and is finite over ζ(Λ).
Use the integral adjoint condition to prove the ideal and conductor inclusions, retaining the actual integral order.
acceptance: For a commutative order, generalized adjoints are ordinary adjugates, so H(Λ)=I(Λ)=Λ.
For Λ=M₂(Z₃), the center and both auxiliary ideals identify with Z₃.
For Λ=Z_p[D_(2p)] with p odd, nr(σ+τ)=(1/p)Σ_g g lies in I(Λ) but not ζ(Λ); forcing all norms into the integral center is false.
For finite Z_p[G], H(Λ)=ζ(Λ) iff p does not divide |G′|, as in Proposition 3.8; this is not the condition p∤|G|.

sources.locator: §2.2 and Example 2.8, pp. 8–9; §3.1, pp. 11–12; Proposition 3.8, p. 13
sources.match: Defines the norm integrality ring and adjoint denominator ideal and explains the conductor relation.

nodes.title: Maximal noncommutative Fitting invariant
nodes.statement: For a finite presentation Λ^a --h→ Λ^b→M→0 of a left module (row vectors, h acts on the right), put Fitt_Λ(h)=0 if a<b and otherwise take the I(Λ)-ideal generated by reduced norms of all b×b row submatrices. This invariant can depend on the presentation. Define Fitt_Λ^max(M) as the largest such ideal among all finite presentations; it exists by noetherianity and the ability to enlarge presentations. It is an I(Λ)-ideal in ζ(A), not in general an ideal of ζ(Λ). An epimorphism M→N gives Fitt^max(M)⊆Fitt^max(N).
hypotheses: Λ a Fitting order; M finitely presented; matrix convention for left modules as stated.
proofSteps: Take norms of all maximal square submatrices and generate an ideal in the integrality ring.
Compare enlarged presentations and use noetherianity to obtain a maximal invariant independent of a chosen presentation.
For a surjection adjoin its kernel’s generators to compare presentations. Do not assert general direct-sum multiplicativity without the extra hypotheses in Nickel’s later sections.
acceptance: For Λ=Z₃ and M=Z₃/9, the maximal invariant is (9); for a free nonzero module it is 0.

For Λ=M₂(Z₃) and M=0, the identity presentation gives I(Λ)=Z₃. The surjective two-block presentation with blocks [[4,1],[1,4]] and [[5,1],[1,5]] has norms 15,24, giving the smaller presentation invariant 3Z₃.
For M=0, Fitt^max(M)=I(Λ); maximizing is essential in the preceding matrix example.
The exact-sequence product inclusion holds, but a general equality for direct sums is not part of this API.

sources.locator: §2.3, Example 2.11, Theorem 2.13, Definition 2.14 and Lemma 2.17, pp. 9–11
sources.match: Defines the presentation invariant, demonstrates dependence and constructs its maximal version.

nodes.title: Fitting invariant of a characteristic class
nodes.statement: Let Λ be a Fitting order with total quotient A and suppose 0→Λ^b --h→Λ^b→M→0 is exact. Then h is invertible over A, ∂[h]=[M] for the NE.2 positive boundary, and Fitt_Λ^max(M)=nr(h)I(Λ). More generally any x∈K₁(A) with ∂x=[M] gives Fitt_Λ^max(M)=nr(x)I(Λ), since changing x by K₁(Λ) changes its reduced norm by an I(Λ)-unit. If a zeta element has ∂ζ=−[M], use nr(ζ⁻¹). Equality of the resulting Fitting ideals does not imply equality of boundary classes or zeta elements.
hypotheses: Λ a Fitting order; M has an injective square finite-free presentation.
For an arbitrary perfect complex with cohomology in several degrees, first specify the virtual/determinant invariant; this theorem concerns the module M.
proofSteps: Apply Nickel Proposition 2.18 to the square presentation.
Use the localization relative triple to compute the boundary sign.
Use exactness of the K₁/relative-K₀ sequence and nr(K₁(Λ))⊆I(Λ)^× to prove independence of the characteristic lift.
acceptance: For Λ=Z_p[[T]], h=(T), obtain Fitt(Λ/T)=(T), not (T⁻¹).
Multiplying h by a Λ-invertible matrix changes its norm by an I(Λ)-unit and leaves the Fitting ideal unchanged.
Equality of fractional ideals permits units of I(Λ) that need not arise from nr K₁(Λ); it is insufficient for equality of relative classes.

sources.match: The square-presentation formula and the one-way K-theory implication are explicit; the converse fails in general.

nodes.title: Denominator-corrected Fitting annihilation
nodes.statement: For every finitely presented module M over a Fitting order Λ, H(Λ)Fitt_Λ^max(M)⊆Ann_(ζ(Λ))(M). Thus a characteristic-element/Fitting formula yields an integral central annihilator only after the stated denominator ideal is applied. For a commutative order H(Λ)=Λ and this reduces to the usual Fitting annihilator inclusion. For noncommutative orders no assertion that the raw reduced norm annihilates M integrally is made.
hypotheses: Λ a Fitting order; M finitely presented; the actual Λ, I(Λ) and H(Λ) are used.
proofSteps: For a chosen presentation use the generalized-adjoint identity to show nr(H) kills the relevant generators after denominator clearing.
Multiply by x∈H(Λ) to make the adjoint entries integral; sum over maximal submatrices and extend to the maximal invariant.
Use H(Λ)I(Λ)=H(Λ) to keep the resulting elements in ζ(Λ).
acceptance: For Z_p/ p^n, the formula gives (p^n)⊆Ann(M), with equality.
For Λ=Z_p[G] and augmentation ideal Δ_pG, the source computes Fitt^max(Δ_pG)=(1/|G′|)N_G Z_p, while the denominator-corrected product is N_G Z_p=Ann_(ζΛ)(Δ_pG).
For G=S₃ and p=3 the raw generator (1/3)N_G is not integral, so an annihilator claim in ζΛ before clearing denominators fails.

sources.match: Proves denominator-corrected annihilation and shows why the integrality factor is necessary.

nodes.title: Exceptional Euler factors and Bockstein leading terms
nodes.statement: Suppose a representation-specialized characteristic function has a proved Laurent factorization f(T)=E(T)g(T), with E a specified product of local Euler factors and g(T)=T^m u(T), u(0)≠0. Write E(T)=T^e v(T), v(0)≠0. Then ord_T f=e+m and the leading coefficient is v(0)u(0). When the specialized perfect complex is semisimple in the Burns–Venjakob sense, identify this coefficient with its Bockstein determinant, retaining the boundary sign and the Γ-generator logarithmic conversion to an s-derivative. This conditional comparison separates an explicit local zero from any further zero in g; interpolation away from zeros alone supplies neither semisimplicity nor a regulator.
hypotheses: A proved local factorization and orders e,m; leading coefficients nonzero.
For the determinant assertion, the source’s semisimplicity, rational acyclicity and chosen Bockstein trivialization hypotheses.
proofSteps: Factor the scalar Laurent series and multiply the first nonzero coefficients.
Apply the existing leading-term/characteristic-series and partial-derivative comparisons with the same Γ-coordinate.
For arithmetic exceptional zeros request the local cohomology factorization and nondegenerate height/regulator input; do not infer them from a main-conjecture ideal equality.
acceptance: E(T)=1−(1+T)=−T and g(0)=a≠0 give a simple zero with leading coefficient −a; losing the local sign fails.
For C=[Λ --T→Λ] in degrees −1,0, BV’s characteristic function T⁻¹ has order −1; its shift has order 1 and the inverse leading coefficient, according to the determinant convention.
If E(T)=−T and g(T)=T u(T), the total order is 2; a single local exceptional factor does not prove the global order is 1.

sources.locator: Proposition 3.8, pp. 10–11; Remark 3.15 and Proposition 3.16, pp. 13–15; Theorem 6.7, pp. 33–36
sources.match: Relates scalar order, Bockstein determinant, cyclotomic derivative and the additional height hypotheses.

Schneider §26 supplies ordered valued bases, and §§27–29 supply analytic comparison, but a primary proof that every finitely generated powerful torsion-free pro-p group has the required uniform basis remains to be checked; DDMS is not cleared and was not accessed. NoncommutativeAnalyticDistributions owns L_G, log/exp, and the analytic-structure equivalence routed by PAPER-FU-24. That owner has no registered stage here, so no guessed node id is used.

gaps.detail: The Euler characteristic formula (77) (Coates–Howson, Theorem 1.1) and the Mordell–Weil and Tate–Shafarevich data of E = X₁(11) over ℚ(μ_5), F_1 and F_2 (CFKSV [12], [16]) are quoted, not proved; they belong to the Selmer and Euler-characteristic owners (SelmerIwasawaCohomology), which do not plan them.

gaps.title: CFKSV §5's inputs from Coates–Howson, Venjakob, Schneps and the CM two-variable main conjecture are not planned
gaps.detail: Verified: the proofs of Lemmas 5.3–5.4, Corollary 5.5 and Proposition 5.6 (pp. 199–201) cite [8] and [9] (Coates–Howson; Proposition 2.13, Lemma 2.1, Lemma 2.5, Remark 2.6), [11] (finiteness of H¹(H_F, E_{p^∞})), Venjakob [26], Schneps [28], Rubin [27] and, for the example, [16] (X(E₁/ℚ(μ₅)^cyc) = 0). None is read or planned.

gaps.title: The numerical data for X₁(11) at p = 5 are quoted from Dokchitser–Dokchitser
gaps.detail: CFKSV equations (108)–(115) attribute their numerical L-values and arithmetic data to Dokchitser–Dokchitser. Those computations have not been reproduced, so the node is a consistency check conditional on that table, not an independent numerical proof.

gaps.title: Finite p-adic group-ring Whitehead and logarithm inputs
gaps.detail: The exact finite-group prerequisites used by Kakde are Oliver Theorems 2.5, 2.8–2.10, 6.6, 6.8, 7.4, 11.2, 12.3(4) and Proposition 12.7, with Wall norm and torsion comparisons. The book is not cleared and was not read; the statements are supported only by Kakde’s explicit citations. KTheoryLowDegrees U.3/U.5 must extend its existing scope to these p-adic group-order theorems. Kakde’s Iwasawa-specific proofs of Lemma 66 and Proposition 67 are planned here, not substituted for the finite-level inputs.

gaps.title: Fukaya–Kato's §1 results on Iwasawa algebras and the complex C(F_∞/F) are not freely available
gaps.detail: A cleared primary copy of Fukaya–Kato was not established. Required inputs are Propositions 1.5.1 and 1.5.3 (K₁ continuity and pro-p kernel), Proposition 1.3.7 (localized characteristic isomorphism), and the perfection/base-change theorem for the dual arithmetic complex with possible p-torsion. The zeta statement is taken as a conjectural contract from Burns–Venjakob Conjecture 4.1; it never supplies existence. Noncommutative finite generation plus no p-torsion gives the separate finite-global-dimension route in NE.4, but does not discharge the p-torsion case.

gaps.title: BV §6 rests on unread Fukaya–Kato and Nekovář results
gaps.detail: The local epsilon-isomorphism contract uses Fukaya–Kato Propositions 3.3.5, 1.6.5 and 4.2.17, Conjecture 3.4.3 and Theorem 4.2.26 as restated in Burns–Venjakob §6. The arithmetic height comparison uses Nekovář Theorem 11.3.9. These originals were not read; SelmerIwasawaCohomology L2 owns the Selmer constructions, but its checked packet does not supply the requested height theorem; that is an extension request. The statement retains all local, semisimplicity and height assumptions.

gaps.detail: Current Tau Ceti and ProfiniteArithmetic already own pLowerCentralSeries and IsProP.padicPow; current ProfiniteProPGroups Layer 9 owns the completed Z_p group algebra and cyclic coordinate. gaps.title: Filtered Auslander transfer and ramified coefficient proof leaves
gaps.detail: Venjakob Theorems 3.19–3.22 and 3.26–3.30 provide the precise filtered and Iwasawa statements. The general Björk filtered Auslander transfer cited there was not read independently, nor was the Brumer coefficient generalization. For ramified O, prove the finite-free coefficient comparison and run the DVR filtered argument; do not deduce regularity merely from module finiteness or quote a commutative flatness instance.

gaps.title: Real two-primary arithmetic complex
gaps.detail: No p=2 main theorem is supplied by the odd-prime sources. An admitted two-primary extension needs real-place complete Tate cochains, duality and a bounded perfect replacement with explicit correction terms. Ordinary real-place cohomology is unbounded 2-periodic and is not silently discarded. The comparison node is the exact input contract, not a constructed perfect complex at 2.

gaps.title: Ritter–Weiss earlier logarithmic inputs and SK₁ classification
gaps.detail: The finite-conductor analytic Möbius calculation is supplied by RW arXiv:1001.2091v3 Propositions 4–5, 9 and Lemma 10, and RW2010 §3. Its uniform-g theorem input has the separate proof-audit obligation below. The earlier logarithm/trace inputs remain: RW3 Proposition 11 (integral logarithm and relative surjectivity), Lemma 12 (torsion), RW4 Proposition 9 (a p-power multiple of t is integral), RW5 Propositions 2.2/2.4 and 3.2 (multiplicative lift and torsion correction), and RW8 Lemma 1/Proposition A (restriction). Their use is explicit in RW2010 Lemmas h–k; their original proofs were not independently audited in this revision. RW2026 still requires Lau’s original component classification and the stated D-family SK₁-vanishing hypothesis. None is silently closed.

gaps.title: Unconditional abelian minus comparison and local hypotheses
gaps.detail: Gambheera–Popescu Theorem 6.30 is stated with its published S,T hypotheses and its minus Selmer/1-motive module. Supplier exact sequences and the covariant Z_p-dual action must be formalized before identifying it with another complex. Their Proposition 7.10(3), p. 37, comparison to the Tate module invokes μ=0; the duality in 7.10(2) does not, so that comparison cannot be used to remove μ=0 in a different statement.

gaps.title: Noncommutative Fitting-order and reduced-norm foundations
gaps.detail: IntegralHeckeAndGaloisDeterminants supplies the generic reduced norm; its current roadmap is already upstream. Nickel’s checked survey supplies Fitting-order, integrality-ring, denominator-ideal and annihilation proofs at target level. The survey’s original references for existence of maximal orders, reduced Cayley–Hamilton and maximal Fitting invariants require a primary proof-leaf check. No higher-dimensional noncentral Iwasawa order or arbitrary converse from Fitting equality is asserted.

gaps.title: Arithmetic semisimplicity and exceptional-zero factorization
gaps.detail: The scalar Laurent-factor identity is elementary; its arithmetic application needs the stated local Euler-factor factorization and the source’s nondegenerate height/regulator and semisimplicity hypotheses. A global main-conjecture equality or interpolation at nonzero values does not prove those hypotheses. BV’s Tate/critical-motive comparisons are conditional as specified at their nodes.

gaps.title: Semilocal K₁ and integrality-evidence proof leaves
gaps.detail: CFKSV cites the semilocal units-surject-K₁ theorem of Vaserstein and invokes supporting cases for Conjecture 4.8, including Kato Proposition 8.19. Their precise primary proofs were not checked here. The former is requested from KTheoryLowDegrees U.3; the latter remains evidence for a conjectural predicate, not a claimed general theorem.

gaps.title: Noncommutative radical and finite-group augmentation leaves
gaps.detail: CFKSV Proposition 2.6 uses the two-sided prime radical’s nilpotence for a noetherian ring and compatibility with the central total quotient, citing [24] §§0.2.6 and 2.3.7. The commutative nilradical does not supply this. Lemma 2.5 also needs nilpotence of the augmentation ideal of F_p[Δ] for a finite p-group Δ. No matching statement was found in the pinned libraries by augmentation/nilpotence search. Both statements are precise proof leaves; complete their finite-dimensional/group-ring arguments or import a verified supplier before closing NE.1.

gaps.title: Unprovided determinant and noncommutative localization supplier contracts
gaps.detail: Reading the supplier packets does not close these requests: GeneralAlgebraicKTheory K.4 has the bounded-perfect comparison but no determinant Picard functor; K.5 has relative fibres but not the needed Ore localization theorem; K.3 has resolution but not complete-ideal K₀ invariance; KTheoryLowDegrees U.3 has commutative scope for the cited semilocal determinant results. Add the precise extensions at their owners, with compatible boundary signs.

gaps.title: Generic compact homology and arithmetic control are extension requests
gaps.detail: The checked SelmerIwasawaCohomology L0 packet does not plan continuous compact bar resolutions or their Tor/Ext comparison. L3 cohomology and Shapiro do not automatically give the requested compact homology theorem. L2 supplies Selmer mapping fibres but the specified elliptic control/coinvariant finiteness and Nekovář height comparison are further inputs. The requests are not existing theorems.

gaps.title: Twisted-algebra coefficients beyond the current owner’s field carrier
gaps.detail: InductionRestriction Layer 7 is the owner, but its checked Suggested.lean assumes field coefficients for the twisted algebra. The central-ring instances R=O[[Z]] and localized completions need its coefficient-ring generalization. Import that extension rather than planning a duplicate generic algebra here.

gaps.title: Uniform smoothing in the Ritter–Weiss analytic theorem
gaps.detail: Ritter–Weiss, Congruences between abelian pseudomeasures II, arXiv:1001.2091v3 Theorem p.2, asserts one g with nontrivial cyclotomic transfers for which the entire smoothed Möbius pseudomeasure sum is a trace. Proposition 4 pp.5–6 requires a fixed g for all even locally constant test functions. The explicit special-cusp proof in Propositions 5,9 and Lemma 10 pp.6–11 chooses a conductor for a given test function. This revision verifies that finite-conductor calculation but does not establish the uniform quantifier passage. The analytic basic-congruences node uses the theorem exactly as stated, with this additional proof-audit leaf; neither a per-function cusp choice nor inverse-limit compactness is presented as a proof of a common g. An independent continuation must justify that passage or provide a different proof of the stated uniform trace theorem. This is an audit obligation, not a claim that the theorem is false.

sourceIssues.locator: Proofs of Propositions 116 (p. 84) and 117 (p. 85) (arXiv v3)
sourceIssues.printed: The proof uses a congruence modulo the full integer r_P and then only a size comparison with a stabilizer.
sourceIssues.correction: Use the congruence modulo p^v_p(r_P); the stabilizer order divides this p-part. The exponent difference (r_P/p)(p−1) is divisible by the corresponding Euler totient. The full modulus is false, for p=3 and r_P=15, since 2^10=4 modulo 15.
sourceIssues.reason: The congruence modulo r_P fails when r_P has a prime factor other than p: for [F : ℚ] = 5, p = 3 and d_P = 3, r_P = 15 and 2^{−15} ≡ 2^{−5} (mod 15) would need 2^{10} ≡ 1 (mod 15), but 2^{10} ≡ 4. An inequality r_P ≥ |(W_GP)_y| does not give a congruence modulo |(W_GP)_y| in any case. The p-part version suffices for the conclusion.

sourceIssues.locator: §2.2, p. 6, and Definition 3.14, p. 14 (arXiv v2); published §2.2 pp.170–171, Remark3.5 p.175 and Definition3.14 p.181
sourceIssues.printed: The category generated by a semisimple complex is taken closed under extensions, and then asserted to remain semisimple.
sourceIssues.correction: Generate it using quasi-isomorphisms, shifts and direct sums. Semisimple complexes are not extension closed: the upper triangular matrix with diagonal T and upper entry 1 has cokernel Λ/T², whose Bockstein differential vanishes, although its two diagonal pieces are semisimple.
sourceIssues.reason: Σ^{ss} is not closed under extensions (the source itself notes it fails (iv), Remark 3.5). For R = Λ(Γ) and A· = [R --T--> R] (semisimple, the example in the proof of Proposition 3.8), B· = [R² --M--> R²] with M = ((T, 1), (0, T)) is an extension 0 → A· → B· → A· → 0, so B· ∈ Σ_{A·}; but H^0(B·) ≅ R/T², κ_0 : (R/T²)^Γ → (R/T²)_Γ is zero, and the Bockstein complex of B· is ℤ_p in degrees 0 and 1 with zero differential, so B· ∉ Σ^{ss}.
sourceIssues.known: Published §2.2 p.170 repairs the general category condition to (iv′), but the definition of Σ_C on p.171 still uses (iv), and Definition3.14 p.181 still asserts Σ_A⊂Σ_ss−ρ. The latter defect remains.

review.reason: For C₂ the sign character is Ind_1^C₂(1)−1 and is the character of an actual one-dimensional representation. Its value at the nonidentity element is−1, while every permutation character counts fixed points and is nonnegative. Thus n_ρ=1 in the displayed integer-combination formula does not characterize permutation characters.

sourceIssues.locator: arXiv:1008.0142v3, Proposition 98, (12), p.69; Proposition 116, pp.84–85
sourceIssues.printed: The zeta function for a cyclic P is congruent modulo its Weyl trace ideal to the unweighted sum of φ(ζ_{P′}) over cyclic P′ with P′^p=P. The proof cancels the fixed-pair contribution as if there were one such P′.
sourceIssues.correction: Replace this analytic branch by full subgroup Möbius sums, with all multiplicities, rather than assuming (12). The main-conjecture target is unchanged.
sourceIssues.reason: Take G=C_{p²}×Γ, Z=Γ^p and P=pC_{p²}×0 in G/Z. The p distinct cyclic overgroups P′=〈(1,t)〉, t∈C_p, all satisfy P′^p=P. Since G is abelian, T_P=p²Λ(U_P)_S, and M3 gives φ(ζ_{P′})≡ζ_P modulo p for each P′. Reducing (12) modulo p would give ζ_P≡pζ_P=0, impossible for a unit. This setting is realized by the compositum of the cyclotomic tower of Q and a disjoint cyclic degree-p² totally real abelian extension; its μ vanishes. In the proposed fixed-pair proof, the pair (β, b)=(a,O_L) at rational positive a, with identity Artin coset, is fixed by the whole group and contributes multiplicity 1−p modulo p rather than 0.

sourceIssues.reason: The U-operator formula at the standard cusp does not imply its constant-term formula at an arbitrary cusp. sourceIssues.printed: The order r of the unshifted cyclotomic Selmer complex is identified with the positive dimension h of H¹_f(Q,W).
sourceIssues.correction: For the unshifted Selmer complex r=−h. For the shifted complex SC[1], whose determinant is the target of the global composite, r=h. Keep the latter in the normalized interpolation formula.
sourceIssues.reason: Under (D2) the special fiber is concentrated in degrees 1,2 and the height B¹ is an isomorphism. Over the T-adic DVR, semisimplicity decomposes the torsion complex into T-blocks in degrees 1,2; each has ordinary cohomology only in degree 2 and contributes (−1)^{2+1}=−1 to BV Definition 3.2. Thus h such blocks have r=−h. Equivalently SC=[R --T→R] in degrees 1,2 has characteristic T⁻¹ with the identity trivialization, so its order is −1, not +1. Shifting negates it.

sourceIssues.printed: The positive power c_γ^m multiplies the global leading term, while the map supplied by the conjecture has inverse compact-support determinant as its codomain.
sourceIssues.correction: After the explicit determinant shift D=RΓ_c[1], the given global map is ζ_D:1→d(D), r(D)=−m and c_γ^(−m)[D,ζ_D]^*=L^*_{p,S}(1,ρ). The global map itself is transported, not inverted.
sourceIssues.reason: For rank one let B²=−ℓ/c_γ in bases of H²_c,H³_c. In the inverse line the Bockstein trivialization is −c_γ/ℓ. Formula (21) gives ζ=L^*_S(1,1)ℓ in these same bases. The leading sign is −1, so the pair on D has coefficient c_γ L^*_S(1,1); normalization needs c_γ⁻¹. More generally its value scales by a^m when γ changes to γ^a, while the normalized p-adic residue is generator independent. A factor c_γ^m would scale by a^{2m}. This is the consequence of repairing E28 with the specified shift, not a claim about an already well-typed alternative convention.
